domain.title: Digital Design & RTL
domain.tag: SystemVerilog · timing · CDC · assertions · synthesis · FPGA & ASIC
domain.why: Every chip that runs an AI model started as someone describing digital logic in a hardware design language, long before it became physical silicon. This domain is where you learn that language from zero — it's deliberately one of the more syntax-heavy parts of the path, because here the language really is the tool. It's also one of the widest doors from software into hardware: writing tests that check a chip design behaves correctly is genuinely software engineering, just aimed at hardware.

concepts.t: Gates, truth tables, and functional completeness
concepts.L1: A gate is a Boolean function realised as a circuit with a propagation delay. A set of gates is functionally complete if every Boolean function can be built from it alone; {NAND} and {NOR} each are, which is why they are the primitive cells a standard-cell library is built around.
concepts.L2: People assume AND is cheaper than NAND because it is 'simpler'. In static CMOS the opposite holds: a NAND is four transistors, and an AND is that same NAND plus a two-transistor inverter. Non-inverting logic costs more area and one more gate delay than the inverting logic it wraps.
concepts.L3: Completeness is proved constructively. Any Boolean function has a canonical sum-of-products form built from NOT, AND and OR. NAND gives NOT directly by tying both inputs together: $\mathrm{NAND}(a,a) = \lnot(a \land a) = \lnot a$. AND follows by inverting a NAND. OR follows from DeMorgan: $a \lor b = \lnot(\lnot a \land \lnot b)$, which is a NAND of two NAND-built inverters. Having all three, every function is reachable. NOR is complete by the dual argument. XOR is not complete on its own - it is linear over GF(2), so no composition of XORs can produce AND.

L4.prompt_tpl: Express `a | b` using only 2-input NAND gates. How many NAND gates does it take, and what is the gate depth?
L4.answer: Three NANDs, depth 2. n1 = ~(a & a) = ~a; n2 = ~(b & b) = ~b; out = ~(n1 & n2) = ~(~a & ~b) = a | b by DeMorgan. n1 and n2 are in parallel (depth 1) and the final NAND is depth 2.
L4.explanation: This is the standard NAND realisation of OR. It also shows why an OR costs more than a NAND in a real library: you pay for two inverters that a NAND-native netlist would not need.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these gate sets is NOT functionally complete on its own?
L4.answer: {XOR, XNOR}
L4.explanation: XOR is linear over GF(2): any XOR network computes an affine function $c_0 \oplus \bigoplus c_i x_i$. AND is not affine, so no XOR/XNOR network can produce it. NAND and NOR are each complete; {AND, NOT} is complete because OR follows from DeMorgan.
options: {NAND}
{XOR, XNOR}
{AND, NOT}

concepts.L1: Boolean algebra is the rewrite system every synthesis tool runs on your RTL. DeMorgan's laws are the two that matter most in practice: they let a bubble on a gate's output be pushed to its inputs, converting between AND-shaped and OR-shaped logic without changing the function.
concepts.L2: DeMorgan is an equality over values, not over circuits. The two forms have identical truth tables but different delay, area and glitch behaviour, so rewriting by DeMorgan changes the netlist even though it cannot change the function. Over four-state values the identities hold only where no operand is X or Z.
concepts.L3: Bubble pushing is what makes DeMorgan a design tool rather than a fact. CMOS gives you inverting gates for free, so a designer draws logic as alternating NAND and NOR stages and uses DeMorgan to check the function still matches. Concretely, an AND-OR structure $\,(a \land b) \lor (c \land d)$ equals $\lnot(\lnot(a \land b) \land \lnot(c \land d))$, which is NAND-NAND: two 2-input NANDs feeding a third. Same function, one fewer inverter pair, same depth. Synthesis does this automatically, but you need it by hand when reading a netlist, reasoning about an active-low signal, or deciding whether `rst_n` should gate with AND or OR.

L4.prompt_tpl: Simplify `(a & b) | (a & ~b) | (~a & b)` to the minimum number of literals and name the identities used.
L4.answer: a | b. Combining on the first two terms: (a & b) | (a & ~b) = a. Then absorption/combining with the third: a | (~a & b) = (a | ~a) & (a | b) = a | b. Two literals.
L4.explanation: The step a | (~a & b) = a | b is worth memorising - it is the identity most often missed by hand, and it is why a redundant qualifying term disappears in synthesis.

L4.prompt_tpl: In four-state SystemVerilog with `a = {a}` and `b = 1'bx`, what does `~(a & b)` evaluate to, and what does `~a | ~b` evaluate to?
L4.answer: For a=0: ~(0 & x) = ~0 = 1, and ~0 | ~x = 1 | x = 1. Both 1. For a=1: ~(1 & x) = ~x = x, and ~1 | ~x = 0 | x = x. Both x. They agree here, but the general point stands that four-state operators are defined by tables, not by algebra.
L4.explanation: SystemVerilog's & and | have explicit four-state truth tables: 0 & x = 0 and 1 | x = 1 are the 'controlling value' cases that keep X from spreading. Algebraic identities that assume two-valued logic can fail once X is involved, which is why gate-level simulation catches things RTL simulation does not.

prereqs: Gates, truth tables, and functional completeness

concepts.L1: Every Boolean function has exactly one canonical sum-of-products form: the OR of the minterms on which it is true. This is the bridge from a specification (a truth table) to a circuit, and it is why $\Sigma m(\ldots)$ notation appears in every textbook and every synthesis paper.
concepts.L2: Canonical form is unique but almost never minimal: it spends one full-width product per true row, so a function true on half of $n$ inputs needs $2^{n-1}$ terms. It is a correctness-preserving starting point, not an implementation - which is why you write the case statement and let synthesis minimise.
concepts.L3: The uniqueness argument: the $2^{n}$ minterms over $n$ variables are pairwise disjoint - $m_{i} \land m_{j} = 0$ for $i \neq j$ - and their OR is the constant 1. So any function decomposes as $f = \bigvee_{i} f(i) \land m_{i}$, and since each $m_{i}$ is 1 on exactly one row, the coefficients $f(i)$ are forced. Two different minterm sets therefore give different truth tables. The dual construction over maxterms $M_{i} = \lnot m_{i}$ gives the canonical product-of-sums, and $f = \Sigma m(S)$ implies $f = \Pi M(\bar{S})$ over the complementary index set.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 3-input function is given as $f = \Sigma m({s})$. Write the equivalent product-of-sums index set $\Pi M(\cdot)$.
L4.answer: The complement of the minterm set within {0..7}. For Sigma m(1,3,6,7) it is Pi M(0,2,4,5); for Sigma m(0,2,5) it is Pi M(1,3,4,6,7); for Sigma m(2,3,4) it is Pi M(0,1,5,6,7).
L4.explanation: The two canonical forms carry the same information: minterms list the rows where f is 1, maxterms list the rows where f is 0. Over $n$ variables the index sets always partition $\{0, \ldots, 2^{n}-1\}$.

L4.prompt_tpl: Over {n} input variables, how many distinct minterms are there, and how many distinct Boolean functions? Answer with the number of distinct minterms.
L4.answer: Minterms: 2**n. Functions: 2**(2**n). For n=3: 8 minterms, 256 functions. For n=4: 16 minterms, 65536 functions. For n=5: 32 minterms, 4294967296 functions.
L4.explanation: Each function is a free choice of 0 or 1 for each of the $2^{n}$ truth-table rows, giving $2^{2^{n}}$ functions. The double exponential is why exhaustive logic minimisation is hopeless beyond a handful of inputs and why heuristics like Espresso exist.

concepts.L1: A Karnaugh map is a truth table redrawn so that physically adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable. Grouping adjacent 1s into power-of-two rectangles applies the combining identity graphically: each doubling of a group deletes one literal from the product term.
concepts.L2: K-maps are not how chips get minimised - Espresso and its successors are, on functions with hundreds of inputs. Learn K-maps because they make the structure visible: prime implicants, essential ones, and the covering problem. A minimal cover is not unique, and greedily picking the biggest group can miss the minimum.
concepts.L3: Adjacency is the whole mechanism. Two cells differing in one variable $x$ hold minterms $p \land x$ and $p \land \lnot x$; combining gives $p$, one literal shorter, and each further doubling removes another. A group of $2^{k}$ cells in an $n$-variable map yields a term with $n-k$ literals. The edges wrap, because the Gray ordering is cyclic. Minimisation is then two steps: enumerate all maximal groups (the prime implicants), then pick a minimum-cost subset covering every 1 - the unate covering problem, NP-hard in general. Essential prime implicants, those uniquely covering some minterm, must be in every cover, so they go in first.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a 4-variable K-map, a group of {k} adjacent cells reduces a product term to how many literals?
L4.answer: 4 - log2(k). For k=2: 3 literals. For k=4: 2 literals. For k=8: 1 literal. For k=16: 0 literals, i.e. the function is constant 1.
L4.explanation: Each doubling of the group size eliminates exactly one variable, because the group spans both polarities of that variable. A group of all 16 cells means the output does not depend on any input.

L4.prompt_tpl: Minimise $f = \Sigma m(0,1,2,3,4,5)$ over variables a,b,c (a is the MSB, weight 4).
L4.answer: f = ~a | ~b. Minterms 0-3 have a=0, giving the group ~a. Minterms 0,1,4,5 have b=0, giving the group ~b. Together they cover 0,1,2,3,4,5 and no others. Both groups are prime and both are essential (m2/m3 only by ~a, m4/m5 only by ~b).
L4.explanation: Note that the two groups overlap on m0 and m1. Overlapping groups are allowed and often required - a cover need not be a partition. This is a case where the greedy answer and the minimum answer coincide, but they do not always.

concepts.L1: A don't-care is an input combination the specification promises will never occur, or an output whose value nobody observes. Minimisation may assign it either value, so don't-cares only ever shrink the result. In RTL you express one by assigning `1'bx`.
concepts.L2: An `x` assignment is a contract you assert, not a wish. If the impossible input does occur, synthesis has already picked whatever was cheapest and the block behaves arbitrarily, while RTL simulation shows X and may not flag it. That mismatch is the classic passed-simulation, failed-in-lab bug, and why many teams ban `x` in RTL.
concepts.L3: The optimisation gain is real. In the BCD example the six unreachable codes let the tool merge groups that would otherwise be blocked, typically halving the literal count of each segment. Formally, a don't-care set $D$ turns one function into a family: any $f$ with $f_{\mathrm{on}} \subseteq f \subseteq f_{\mathrm{on}} \cup D$ is acceptable, and the minimiser searches that family. The safe engineering position is to assert the promise rather than assume it: keep the don't-care for area, and add a concurrent assertion `assert property (@(posedge clk) d <= 4'd9);` so that any violation of the premise fails loudly in simulation and in formal, instead of silently in the field.

L4.prompt_tpl: A designer writes `default: state_next = 'x;` in an FSM's next-state logic to help area, and the FSM is reachable from an illegal state after a glitch on an asynchronous input. What actually happens on silicon?
L4.answer: Synthesis has already chosen concrete next-state logic for the illegal encodings - whatever minimised the cover - so the FSM jumps to some arbitrary legal or illegal state and may never return to a good one (lockup). Simulation would have shown X and possibly propagated it, but nothing forces the two to agree. The fix is a defined default (usually the reset state) plus an assertion that the illegal encoding never occurs.
L4.explanation: This is the 'safe FSM' argument. Don't-cares are legitimate for pure combinational blocks whose inputs are provably constrained, and dangerous for state that can be corrupted, because a corrupted state has no promise attached to it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 4-input function has {ones} minterms in its ON-set and {dcs} don't-cares. Over how many distinct completely specified functions is the minimiser searching?
L4.answer: 2**dcs. For dcs=6: 64. For dcs=3: 8. For dcs=8: 256. The ON-set size does not affect the count; each don't-care is an independent binary choice.
L4.explanation: The don't-care set defines an interval in the lattice of Boolean functions. A minimiser explores it implicitly through prime-implicant generation rather than by enumeration, which matters once the count is astronomical.

concepts.t: The multiplexer as a universal element
concepts.L1: A multiplexer selects one of several inputs under a select code. It is the direct hardware form of Shannon expansion, $f = s \land f|_{s=1} \lor \lnot s \land f|_{s=0}$, which makes it functionally complete: FPGA LUTs and many ASIC datapaths are mux trees underneath.
concepts.L2: `d[s]` with a variable index reads like an array load but synthesises to a mux tree: every input is driven at once, area is $n-1$ two-input muxes, and delay is $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$. A 64-entry variable index is a real 63-mux structure sitting on the critical path, not the constant-time load a software reader assumes.
concepts.L3: Shannon expansion is the proof and the construction at once. For any $f$ and any variable $s$, $f = (s \land f|_{s=1}) \lor (\lnot s \land f|_{s=0})$, verified by substituting $s=0$ and $s=1$. That expression is exactly a 2:1 mux with select $s$. Recursing on the remaining variables gives a complete binary mux tree of depth $n$ whose $2^{n}$ leaves are the truth-table entries - which is literally what a $2^{n}$-entry LUT in an FPGA is. Building larger muxes from 2:1 cells gives a tree of $n-1$ cells and depth $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$; building them as a flat one-hot AND-OR gives depth 2 but wide gates, and synthesis picks between the two based on the timing constraint.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n}:1 multiplexer is built entirely from 2:1 muxes arranged as a balanced tree. How many 2:1 cells, and what is the depth in mux delays? Answer with the number of 2:1 cells.
L4.answer: Cells: n-1. Depth: ceil(log2(n)). For n=8: 7 cells, depth 3. For n=16: 15 cells, depth 4. For n=64: 63 cells, depth 6.
L4.explanation: The cell count is the internal-node count of a binary tree with n leaves, which is n-1 regardless of shape. Only the depth depends on balance, and it is why a wide variable index is a timing problem, not just an area problem.

L4.prompt_tpl: Implement XOR using exactly one 2:1 mux, given inputs a and b and an inverter.
L4.answer: Put a on the select and use y = a ? ~b : b. When a=0 the mux passes b; when a=1 it passes ~b. That is a ^ b. Only one mux and one inverter are needed.
L4.explanation: This is Shannon expansion about a: XOR restricted to a=0 is b, and restricted to a=1 is ~b. Any 2-input function reduces this way, which is the argument for the mux being functionally complete.

concepts.L1: A decoder expands an $n$-bit code to $2^{n}$ mutually exclusive lines; an encoder is its inverse but is only well defined on one-hot input. A priority encoder removes that restriction by defining an order, returning the index of the highest-priority asserted bit plus a valid flag.
concepts.L2: The `for` loop is not a loop at run time. Synthesis unrolls it fully, and the last iteration that fires wins - so counting down from N-1 makes bit 0 highest priority, and reversing the loop direction silently reverses the priority with no warning. Reviewers miss this constantly because the code reads like software.
concepts.L3: The unrolled form is a chain: `idx` is a cascade of $N$ conditional overrides, so the naive structure has depth proportional to $N$. Real implementations use a parallel-prefix formulation instead. Define the 'no higher-priority request' signal $k_{i} = \lnot \bigvee_{j<i} req_{j}$, computable by a prefix-OR network of depth $\lceil \log_{2} N \rceil$; then the one-hot grant is $g_{i} = req_{i} \land k_{i}$ and the index is a one-hot-to-binary encode. That turns an $O(N)$ chain into $O(\log N)$, which is the difference between a 32-entry arbiter closing timing at 500 MHz and not. Synthesis will often find this itself, but only if you have not written the loop in a way that forces a chain.

L4.prompt_tpl: `always_comb begin if (en) y[a] = 1'b1; end` for a decoder. Two separate defects. Name them.
L4.answer: First, y is not assigned on every path (en=0, and the bits other than y[a]), so a latch is inferred on all N output bits. Second, even when en=1 the previously set bits are never cleared, so y is not one-hot - it accumulates. Both are fixed by assigning y = '0 as the first statement of the block.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common combinational bug in SystemVerilog. `always_comb` will report the latch as a lint error in Verilator and most linters, but only if you run the lint - the code simulates as a latch and often looks right in a short testbench.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a {n}-input priority encoder, how wide is the index output, and what is the depth of a parallel-prefix implementation in gate levels (prefix network only)? Answer with the index output width in bits.
L4.answer: Index width: ceil(log2(n)). Prefix depth: ceil(log2(n)). For n=8: 3 bits, depth 3. For n=16: 4 bits, depth 4. For n=32: 5 bits, depth 5.
L4.explanation: Both quantities are $\lceil \log_{2} n \rceil$ but for different reasons: the index must address $n$ positions, and a prefix-OR over $n$ elements has logarithmic depth. Compare with the naive priority chain, whose depth is $n$.

concepts.L1: A comparator produces equality or magnitude relations; equality is a wide XNOR-and-reduce, magnitude is a subtract whose carry-out and sign are examined. A barrel shifter shifts by an arbitrary run-time amount in one cycle using one mux stage per bit of the shift amount.
concepts.L2: Signedness belongs to the operands, not the operator, and the whole expression decides it. One unsigned operand makes the comparison unsigned: with `a` signed holding -1 and `b` unsigned holding 1, `a < b` is false, because `a` is reinterpreted as 255. Casting one side with `$signed` does not help; both must be signed.
concepts.L3: The barrel shifter's structure comes from writing the shift amount in binary: shifting by $s = \sum_{i} s_{i} 2^{i}$ is the composition of conditional shifts by $2^{i}$. Each stage is $W$ two-input muxes controlled by one bit of $s$, so a 32-bit barrel shifter is 5 stages and $32 \times 5 = 160$ mux cells, with depth 5 rather than the $W$ of a shift-register approach. Rotates use the same network with wraparound wiring; arithmetic right shifts fill with the replicated sign bit. The `genvar` loop above is elaboration-time structural generation - the tool emits five distinct assign statements, one per stage, and the `1 << i` is a compile-time constant in each.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given a signed 8-bit `a` holding -1 and an unsigned 8-bit `b` holding {b}, what does `a < b` evaluate to, and why?
L4.answer: 0 (false). Because b is unsigned, the whole comparison is evaluated unsigned, so a is reinterpreted as 8'hFF = 255, and 255 < b is false for any 8-bit b. Casting both operands with `$signed` makes it 1 (true) for positive b.
L4.explanation: This is the classic width-and-sign trap. The rule is that an expression is signed only if every operand is signed; one unsigned operand poisons the whole expression. Linters flag mixed-sign comparisons for exactly this reason.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {w}-bit barrel shifter built from 2:1 muxes: how many stages, how many mux cells, and what is the mux-delay depth? Answer with the number of mux cells.
L4.answer: Stages and depth: log2(w). Cells: w*log2(w). For w=8: 3 stages, 24 cells. For w=32: 5 stages, 160 cells. For w=64: 6 stages, 384 cells.
L4.explanation: Each stage handles one bit of the shift amount and shifts by a fixed power of two, so the count of stages is the width of the shift-amount field. Area grows as $W \log_{2} W$ while delay grows only as $\log_{2} W$ - a good trade, and the reason barrel shifters are standard in every ALU.

concepts.t: The full adder and ripple-carry delay
concepts.L1: A full adder sums three bits into a two-bit result. Chaining $W$ of them carry-out to carry-in gives a ripple-carry adder: minimum area, and delay linear in $W$ because the carry must physically propagate from bit 0 to bit $W-1$.
concepts.L2: You should not instantiate this. Writing `a + b` lets synthesis choose between ripple, carry-select, and prefix architectures per the timing constraint, and it will pick better than you. Hand-instantiating a ripple-carry adder pins the tool to the slowest option and is a common way to miss $f_{max}$ by a factor of two.
concepts.L3: The delay is the carry chain, not the sum. Once $c_{i}$ is stable, $s_{i}$ costs one XOR; but $c_{i+1}$ needs $c_{i}$, so the chain is $W$ full-adder carry delays deep. With the standard textbook parameter $t_{FA} = 300$ ps, a 32-bit ripple-carry adder takes $32 \times 300 = 9600$ ps, or 9.6 ns - about 104 MHz if that adder is the whole critical path. The XOR structure of the sum is why the carry equation is usually written $c_{out} = (a \land b) \lor (c_{in} \land (a \oplus b))$ rather than the majority form: the $a \oplus b$ term is shared with the sum, so the cell reuses one gate.

L4.prompt_tpl: With a full-adder carry delay of 300 ps per stage, what is the propagation delay of a {w}-bit ripple-carry adder, and the maximum clock frequency if that adder is the entire critical path? Answer with the propagation delay in picoseconds.
L4.answer: Delay = 300*w ps. For w=8: 2400 ps, 416.67 MHz. For w=32: 9600 ps, 104.17 MHz. For w=64: 19200 ps, 52.08 MHz. Frequency is 1/delay with no flop overhead counted.
L4.explanation: The linearity is the point: doubling the width halves the frequency. This is why every real adder wider than about 8 bits uses a lookahead or prefix structure, and why 64-bit integer add is a genuinely hard timing problem in a high-frequency core.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that `cout = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b))` equals the majority function of a, b and cin.
L4.answer: Majority is 1 when at least two inputs are 1. Case a=b=1: first term is 1, majority is 1. Case a=b=0: both terms are 0 (a^b = 0), majority is 0. Case a != b: a&b = 0 and a^b = 1, so the expression is cin, and majority is also cin because exactly one of a,b is already 1. All cases agree.
L4.explanation: The case split on a versus b is the standard proof and it also explains the implementation: when a and b differ the cell is transparent to the carry, which is exactly the propagate condition that carry-lookahead exploits.

concepts.t: Carry-lookahead: generate, propagate, and log depth
concepts.L1: Carry-lookahead breaks the serial carry recurrence by computing, for each bit, whether it generates a carry ($g = a \land b$) or merely propagates one ($p = a \oplus b$). Those signals depend only on the operands, so all of them are available at once and the carries can be formed in parallel.
concepts.L2: The four-bit block is not the content. The real fact is that the carry recurrence is associative under $(g,p) \circ (g',p') = (g \lor p \land g',\ p \land p')$, which turns carry computation into a prefix problem solvable in $\lceil \log_{2} W \rceil$ depth by Kogge-Stone, Brent-Kung or Sklansky networks.
concepts.L3: The Harris and Harris delay model makes the trade concrete. For an $N$-bit adder in $k$-bit lookahead blocks, $t_{CLA} = t_{pg} + t_{pg\_block} + (N/k - 1)\,t_{AND\_OR} + k\,t_{FA}$. With their parameters $t_{pg}=100$, $t_{pg\_block}=600$, $t_{AND\_OR}=300$, $t_{FA}=300$ ps and $N=32$, $k=4$: $100 + 600 + 7 \times 300 + 4 \times 300 = 4000$ ps, against $32 \times 300 = 9600$ ps for ripple - a 2.4 times speedup for roughly 1.5 to 2 times the area. At $N=64$ the same formula gives 6400 ps against 19200 ps, a factor of 3, because the ripple term grows linearly while the lookahead term grows as $N/k$ with a much smaller coefficient.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using the Harris model t_CLA = t_pg + t_pgblock + (N/k - 1)*t_andor + k*t_FA with t_pg=100, t_pgblock=600, t_andor=300 and t_FA=300 ps, compute the delay of a {n}-bit carry-lookahead adder with k = 4, and its speedup over ripple-carry. Answer with the carry-lookahead delay in picoseconds.
L4.explanation: The speedup grows with width because the ripple term is $N t_{FA}$ while the lookahead term is $(N/k) t_{AND\_OR}$ plus constants. Hierarchical lookahead - blocks of blocks - replaces the linear $N/k$ term with another logarithm.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that the carry operator `(g,p) o (g2,p2) = (g | (p & g2), p & p2)` is associative, and say why that matters.
L4.answer: Expand both groupings. Left: ((g,p) o (g',p')) o (g'',p'') has generate g | p&g' | p&p'&g'' and propagate p&p'&p''. Right: (g,p) o ((g',p') o (g'',p'')) has generate g | p&(g' | p'&g'') = g | p&g' | p&p'&g'' and propagate p&(p'&p''). Identical. It matters because an associative operator over a sequence can be evaluated by a parallel-prefix network of depth log2(N) instead of a serial chain of depth N.
L4.explanation: This is the whole theory of fast adders in one line. Kogge-Stone, Brent-Kung, Han-Carlson and Sklansky are all just different prefix networks for the same associative operator, trading depth against wiring and fanout.

prereqs: The full adder and ripple-carry delay

concepts.L1: A carry-save adder adds three numbers to a redundant two-vector form (sum and carry) in one full-adder delay, independent of width, because carries are stored rather than propagated. It is the building block of every fast multiplier and every multi-operand accumulator.
concepts.L2: The redundant form is not a number you can test. $s$ and $c$ jointly represent a value; equality, magnitude and sign are undefined until they collapse. A carry-save accumulator still pays one full carry-propagate adder before any branch or comparison, which is why MAC pipelines defer the collapse to the end.
concepts.L3: The invariant is the proof. For each bit position, the full adder writes $x_{i} + y_{i} + z_{i} = s_{i} + 2 c_{i}$, where $s_{i}$ is the XOR and $c_{i}$ the majority. Summing over positions with weights $2^{i}$: $\sum 2^{i}(x_{i}+y_{i}+z_{i}) = \sum 2^{i} s_{i} + \sum 2^{i+1} c_{i}$, i.e. $x + y + z = s + 2c$. Nothing crosses bit positions, so the delay is one cell regardless of $W$. Chaining compressors reduces $n$ addends toward two: each level maps three rows to two, so $n$ rows become roughly $2n/3$, and reaching two rows takes about $\log_{1.5} n$ levels - 8 levels for 32 rows, against 31 sequential adds.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must sum {n} equally weighted W-bit numbers using only 3:2 compressors until two rows remain, then one carry-propagate adder. How many compression levels, and how many CSA cell rows? Answer with the number of CSA rows.
L4.answer: Levels are found by repeatedly mapping r rows to 2*floor(r/3) + (r mod 3). For n=8: 4 levels. For n=16: 6 levels. For n=32: 8 levels. Cell count is (n-2) CSA rows in total, since each compressor removes exactly one row.
L4.explanation: Each 3:2 compressor consumes three rows and produces two, so it removes exactly one row: reducing n rows to 2 always takes n-2 compressors regardless of arrangement. Only the depth depends on how you arrange them, which is what a Wallace tree optimises.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accumulator holds a running sum in carry-save form for throughput. What must happen before the design can test `if (acc == 0)`, and what does that cost?
L4.answer: The redundant pair must be collapsed with a carry-propagate adder: acc_value = s + (c << 1). Only then is a comparison meaningful, because s and c individually carry no ordering information. The cost is one full adder delay of log2(W) depth, which is exactly the latency carry-save was avoiding - so the collapse is placed once, at the end, not inside the loop.
L4.explanation: This is the standard reason MAC and dot-product datapaths keep accumulation redundant and only normalise at the output. Any comparison, saturation check or branch on the accumulator forces a collapse and reintroduces the carry chain you were dodging.

prereqs: The full adder and ripple-carry delay

concepts.L1: An array multiplier computes all $W$ partial products in parallel - each is the multiplicand ANDed with one multiplier bit and shifted - and then sums them. The AND array is one gate delay; all the cost is in the summation network.
concepts.L2: The width rule catches everyone. In SystemVerilog the result width of `a * b` comes from the assignment context, not the natural $2W$. An 8-bit destination silently keeps only the low 8 bits, and `(a * b) >> 8` truncates to the context width before it shifts, so the bits you wanted are already gone.
concepts.L3: Area is why multipliers are scarce. The AND array is $W^{2}$ gates and the summation network is $O(W^{2})$ full adders, so a $W$-bit multiplier is roughly an order of magnitude larger than a $W$-bit adder - the common rule of thumb is about ten times for 32 bits. Delay for the naive chain is $O(W)$ adder delays because partial products are summed sequentially; the Wallace tree cuts that to $O(\log W)$. This quadratic area is exactly why ML accelerators quantise: an int8 multiplier is about one sixteenth the area of an int32 one, so the same silicon buys sixteen times the MAC count, which is the entire economic argument for low-precision inference.

L4.prompt_tpl: `logic [{w}-1:0] a, b; logic [{w}-1:0] p; assign p = a * b;` The product is wrong for large operands. Why, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: The result of a * b is computed in the width of the assignment context, which here is w bits, so the top w bits of the true 2w-bit product are discarded. For w=8, 200*200 = 40000 = 16'h9C40, and p gets 8'h40 = 64. The fix is to declare p as [2*w-1:0], or to widen an operand first, e.g. assign p = {{{w}{1'b0}}, a} * b, when the destination is narrower than 2w.
L4.explanation: SystemVerilog's context-determined expression widths are the single most common source of silent arithmetic bugs. Verilator's WIDTHTRUNC and WIDTHEXPAND warnings catch this, which is a strong argument for running lint as an error gate.

L4.prompt_tpl: Roughly how many times more MAC units fit in fixed area if you move from int{hi} multipliers to int{lo}, assuming multiplier area scales with the square of the operand width?
L4.answer: Ratio is (hi/lo)**2. For hi=32, lo=8: 16 times. For hi=16, lo=8: 4 times. For hi=32, lo=4: 64 times. Real ratios are smaller because accumulators, registers and interconnect do not shrink quadratically.
L4.explanation: This quadratic scaling is the whole economic case for quantised inference: the same die area buys 16 times the int8 MACs it buys int32 MACs. It is also why accumulation is kept wider than multiplication - the accumulator is linear in width, so widening it is cheap.

concepts.L1: Booth recoding rewrites the multiplier in a redundant signed-digit form so that runs of ones collapse. Radix-4 (modified Booth) consumes two multiplier bits per partial product, halving the number of rows the summation tree must reduce, and it handles two's-complement operands natively.
concepts.L2: Halving the rows does not halve the delay. Tree depth is logarithmic in row count, so 32 rows down to 17 saves about one reduction level, not half. The wins are area - half the partial-product generators - and native two's-complement operation. Against that, each row now needs a 5:1 select and a negate.
concepts.L3: The identity is $\sum_{i} b_{i} 2^{i} = \sum_{j} (b_{2j-1} + b_{2j} - 2 b_{2j+1}) 4^{j}$ with $b_{-1} = 0$. The bracket takes values in $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$, which is exactly the action table: those are the only multiples of $a$ needed, and each is a shift plus an optional two's-complement negation. Negation is implemented as bitwise inversion plus a 1 injected at the row's least significant position, so it costs no extra adder. For a 32-bit multiplier the row count is $\lceil (32+1)/2 \rceil = 17$ rather than 32, and a Wallace reduction of 17 rows needs 7 levels against 8 for 32 rows.

L4.prompt_tpl: Radix-4 Booth on a {w}-bit multiplier: how many partial products, and how many 3:2 reduction levels does a Wallace tree need for that many rows versus the unrecoded count? Answer with the number of partial products.
L4.answer: Partial products: ceil((w+1)/2). For w=8: 5 rows, 3 levels versus 8 rows at 4 levels. For w=16: 9 rows, 5 levels versus 16 rows at 6 levels. For w=32: 17 rows, 7 levels versus 32 rows at 8 levels. Roughly half the rows for one fewer level.
L4.explanation: The asymmetry between area and delay is the point: Booth buys area cheaply and depth expensively, because depth is logarithmic in the row count. Most designs use it anyway, for the area and for native signed operation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Recode the 8-bit multiplier value 0b00111100 with radix-4 Booth and give the resulting partial-product actions from the least significant window upward.
L4.explanation: The run of four ones collapses to one subtract and one add, which is the classic Booth win. Long runs of ones are exactly the case where the unrecoded form wastes rows.

concepts.L1: A Wallace tree arranges carry-save adders so that partial-product rows are reduced greedily, three at a time, in parallel. Depth grows logarithmically rather than linearly in the number of rows, turning an $O(W)$ multiplier into an $O(\log W)$ one.
concepts.L2: Wallace and Dadda have identical depth and differ in cell count. Wallace compresses as early as possible, spending more full adders for a narrower final adder; Dadda compresses only as much as each level needs, using fewer cells but a wider final adder. Neither wins universally, and no tool tells you which it picked.
concepts.L3: The recurrence is $r_{k+1} = 2\lfloor r_{k}/3 \rfloor + (r_{k} \bmod 3)$: each group of three rows becomes two, and up to two leftover rows pass through. Starting from 32 rows the sequence is 32, 22, 15, 10, 7, 5, 4, 3, 2 - eight levels. Compare 31 sequential adder delays for the naive array. The compressor count is invariant: every 3:2 cell removes exactly one row, so reducing $n$ rows to 2 costs $n-2$ rows of cells no matter how they are arranged; only depth depends on the schedule. The final carry-propagate adder is unavoidable and, at 64 bits wide, is usually the longest single stage in the multiplier.

L4.prompt_tpl: Apply the reduction `r -> 2*(r/3) + (r mod 3)` with integer division, starting from {n} rows. List the sequence and give the level count to reach 2 rows.
L4.explanation: Doubling the row count adds only about two levels, which is the logarithmic behaviour. Note 16 and 17 rows take the same depth - the reason radix-4 Booth on a 32-bit operand (17 rows) is close in depth to a 16-row tree.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compared with a Wallace tree of the same row count, a Dadda tree has:
L4.answer: the same depth but fewer compressor cells and a wider final adder
L4.explanation: Dadda defers compression until a level would otherwise exceed the maximum height that still meets the target depth. That saves full adders in the tree but leaves a wider redundant pair for the final carry-propagate adder to absorb.
options: lower depth and fewer cells
the same depth but fewer compressor cells and a wider final adder
higher depth but a narrower final adder

sections.note: where the clock enters, and where every performance number comes from

concepts.L1: A latch passes its input straight through while its enable is asserted and holds when it deasserts. A flip-flop samples only at a clock edge, so its output changes once per cycle. Almost all synchronous design uses flip-flops; latches appear deliberately only in a few low-power and time-borrowing styles.
concepts.L2: Latches are not banned for being exotic - they are banned because timing analysis of transparent logic is hard. A latch lets a path borrow time from the next cycle, so closure stops being a per-stage check and becomes a global one. Most flows therefore treat any inferred latch as an error.
concepts.L3: The master-slave construction is why an edge-triggered flop exists at all. Two level-sensitive latches sit in series with inverted enables: while $clk = 0$ the master tracks $d$ and the slave holds; at the rising edge the master closes and the slave opens, passing the captured value. Because the two are never transparent at once, there is no combinational path from $d$ to $q$ - which is what makes a synchronous pipeline analysable one stage at a time. It also explains setup and hold: setup is the master's requirement that $d$ be stable before it closes, hold that $d$ stay stable long enough for the closure to complete.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design contains an inferred latch on a data path. Which statement is the strongest reason to fix it?
L4.answer: It makes static timing analysis borrow time across cycle boundaries, so per-stage timing closure no longer holds
L4.explanation: Latches are smaller than flops and can be functionally correct, so area and correctness are not the argument. The problem is analysability: transparency lets a path start in one cycle and finish in the next, which breaks the simple arrival-versus-required check that STA on flop-to-flop paths relies on.
options: A latch uses more area than a flip-flop
It makes static timing analysis borrow time across cycle boundaries, so per-stage timing closure no longer holds
Latches cannot be reset

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can a master-slave flip-flop have no combinational path from d to q, given that both of its latches are transparent for half a cycle each?
L4.answer: Because the two latches are enabled on opposite phases, so they are never transparent at the same instant. While clk is low the master tracks d and the slave is opaque; while clk is high the slave tracks the master's held value and the master is opaque. Every path from d to q therefore passes through at least one closed latch at all times.
L4.explanation: This is the whole reason edge-triggered design is analysable: the flop is an opaque boundary in both phases, so a pipeline stage's timing depends only on its own logic, not on what the next stage does.

concepts.t: Setup time, hold time, and clock-to-Q
concepts.L1: Setup and hold define a window around the clock edge in which the flop's data input must not change. Clock-to-Q is how long after the edge the output settles. These three library numbers, plus the combinational delay between flops, determine every frequency claim a design makes.
concepts.L2: Hold analysis uses contamination clock-to-Q - the earliest the launching flop can start moving - and minimum logic delay, not the maximum numbers setup uses. Mixing them is the classic error and makes hold violations look impossible when they are not. Setup signs off at the slow corner, hold at the fast one.
concepts.L3: The window exists because the capturing latch inside the flop needs time to resolve. If $d$ moves inside it, the internal node is driven toward both states at once and the flop can go metastable or latch the wrong value. Setup and hold are characterised, not derived: the vendor sweeps data arrival against the clock and records where clock-to-Q degrades by a criterion, usually 10 per cent. That is why the numbers depend on transition time, load, voltage and temperature, and why a report shows different setup values on different instances of one cell. They are statistical thresholds, not walls - a marginal violation stretches $t_{cq}$ before it causes failure.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which pair of delays is used for a hold check between two flops on the same clock?
L4.answer: Minimum (contamination) clock-to-Q of the launch flop and minimum combinational delay
L4.explanation: Hold asks whether new data can arrive at the capture flop too soon, so it uses the fastest possible path: earliest launch and shortest logic. Setup asks whether data arrives too late, so it uses the slowest. Using maximum numbers for hold is the standard error and hides real violations.
options: Maximum clock-to-Q and maximum combinational delay
Minimum (contamination) clock-to-Q of the launch flop and minimum combinational delay
Maximum clock-to-Q and minimum combinational delay

L4.prompt_tpl: Setup and hold are characterised by sweeping data arrival and watching clock-to-Q. What practical consequence does that have for a path that misses setup by 5 ps?
L4.answer: It will probably still work, but with degraded clock-to-Q. The library setup number is the arrival time at which t_cq has already stretched by a chosen criterion, typically 10 percent, so a small violation means a slightly slower flop rather than an immediate failure. It is still a real risk because the degradation is nonlinear and the margin was there to absorb process, voltage, temperature and ageing variation.
L4.explanation: This is why timing signoff uses margin rather than a hard boundary, and why 'it works on the bench' is not evidence that a negative-slack path is safe. The failure becomes probabilistic and temperature-dependent, which is the worst kind of bug to debug in the field.

concepts.t: The setup equation and maximum frequency
concepts.L1: The setup equation says a clock period must cover the launching flop's clock-to-Q, the combinational delay between the flops, the capturing flop's setup requirement, and any clock skew working against you. Maximum frequency is its reciprocal, and slack is how much room is left.
concepts.L2: $f_{max}$ is set by the single worst path, not by an average. That is why a 390 MHz design often reaches 460 MHz by pipelining one adder: 400 ps off one path moves the period from 2560 to 2160 ps. It also means logic added anywhere off the critical path is free - the opposite of the software intuition that all work costs time.
concepts.L3: Every term is a physical fact about one path. With $t_{cq} = 150$, $t_{logic} = 2200$, $t_{su} = 90$ and $t_{skew} = 120$ ps, $T_{clk} \geq 2560$ ps, so $f_{max} = 1/(2.56\ \mathrm{ns}) = 390.625$ MHz. Cut the logic to 1800 ps and the period becomes 2160 ps, or 462.96 MHz - a 18.5 per cent gain from a 400 ps saving, because the fixed overhead of 360 ps does not shrink. That fixed overhead is why pipelining has diminishing returns: as $t_{logic}$ falls toward $t_{cq} + t_{su} + t_{skew}$, each extra stage buys less and less while adding a cycle of latency and a register file's worth of area and power.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given clock-to-Q 150 ps, setup 90 ps, skew 120 ps and combinational delay {tl} ps, compute the minimum clock period and the maximum frequency. Answer with the minimum clock period in picoseconds.
L4.explanation: The fixed 360 ps of flop and skew overhead is the reason pipelining saturates: once t_logic is comparable to that overhead, halving the logic no longer nearly doubles the frequency.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design has clock-to-Q 150 ps, setup 90 ps, skew 120 ps and a 2200 ps critical path. You split the logic into two equal stages. What is the new f_max, and why is it not double?
L4.answer: Each stage now has 1100 ps of logic, so T = 150 + 1100 + 90 + 120 = 1460 ps and f_max = 684.93 MHz. The old value was 390.625 MHz, so the gain is 1.753x, not 2x, because the 360 ps of flop and skew overhead is paid once per stage and does not halve. Latency also rises from one cycle to two.
L4.explanation: This is the pipelining law in one calculation: speedup is (t_logic + C)/(t_logic/n + C) with C the per-stage overhead, which tends to (t_logic/C + 1) rather than to n. Beyond a handful of stages you are mostly buying flops.

prereqs: Setup time, hold time, and clock-to-Q

concepts.L1: A hold violation means new data reaches the capture flop before the old data has been safely latched - the path is too fast, not too slow. The check involves only the fastest launch, the shortest logic and the hold requirement, so it is entirely independent of clock frequency.
concepts.L2: Because hold is frequency-independent, a hold violation on a taped-out chip is unfixable - you cannot slow, cool or undervolt out of it. A setup failure gives a slower chip; a hold failure gives a broken one. That asymmetry is why hold closes with pessimistic margin and why physical design inserts delay buffers by the thousand.
concepts.L3: The equation contains no period because both flops sample the same edge. Data launched by edge $n$ must not corrupt the value that the capture flop is latching at edge $n$. The earliest that data can arrive is $t_{ccq} + t_{logic,min}$ after the launch clock, and the capture flop needs its input stable until $t_{h}$ after its own clock, which arrives $t_{skew}$ later. With $t_{ccq}=80$, $t_{logic,min}=30$, $t_{h}=100$ and $t_{skew}=60$ ps: $110 \geq 160$ is false, so slack is $-50$ ps. Adding a 60 ps buffer on the data path makes it $170 \geq 160$, slack $+10$ ps - and costs nothing in setup, because the setup path had 2200 ps of slack to spare.

L4.prompt_tpl: With contamination clock-to-Q {tccq} ps, minimum logic delay {tmin} ps, hold requirement 100 ps and clock skew 60 ps, compute the hold slack and state whether it passes. Answer with the hold slack in picoseconds.
L4.answer: Slack = tccq + tmin - (100 + 60). For tccq=80, tmin=30: 110 - 160 = -50 ps, fails. For tccq=80, tmin=120: 200 - 160 = +40 ps, passes. For tccq=150, tmin=30: 180 - 160 = +20 ps, passes.
L4.explanation: Note that the clock period never enters the calculation. A hold failure at 100 MHz is still a hold failure at 1 MHz, which is why it must be closed in physical design and cannot be worked around in the lab.

L4.prompt_tpl: A prototype chip fails intermittently. Lowering the clock from 400 MHz to 100 MHz does not help; raising the supply voltage makes it worse. What is the most likely cause?
L4.answer: A hold violation
L4.explanation: Frequency-independence points at hold rather than setup. Raising the voltage makes logic faster, which shortens the data path further and worsens hold - the opposite of the effect on setup. That combination of symptoms is close to diagnostic.
options: A setup violation on the critical path
A hold violation
Insufficient decoupling capacitance

prereqs: The setup equation and maximum frequency

concepts.L1: Clock skew is the difference in clock arrival time between two flops. It is deterministic and spatial: the same two flops always see the same skew. It appears in both the setup and hold equations, which is why reducing skew is not always the right move.
concepts.L2: Skew is not uniformly bad. If the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock the path gets a longer effective period, helping setup while hurting hold - and clock-tree synthesis exploits that deliberately. What is uniformly bad is uncontrolled skew, because the tool must then assume the worst case on every path at once.
concepts.L3: The sign convention is what people get wrong, so anchor it. Let $t_{L}$ and $t_{C}$ be clock arrival at launch and capture, and $\delta = t_{C} - t_{L}$. The capture edge lands at $t_{L} + T_{clk} + \delta$, so setup becomes $T_{clk} + \delta \geq t_{cq} + t_{logic} + t_{su}$: positive $\delta$ helps. Hold compares against the same edge $t_{L} + \delta$, giving $t_{ccq} + t_{logic,min} \geq t_{h} + \delta$: positive $\delta$ hurts. Useful skew pushes $\delta$ positive on a critical stage, and the next stage pays by the same amount. The budget is conserved around any loop in the clock tree.

L4.prompt_tpl: A pipeline stage misses setup by 80 ps. Clock-tree synthesis delays the capture flop's clock by 120 ps. What happens to this stage's setup slack, to its hold slack, and to the next stage?
L4.answer: Setup slack on this stage improves by 120 ps, so it goes from -80 to +40 ps and passes. Hold slack on this stage worsens by 120 ps and may now fail, requiring buffer insertion. The next stage sees its launch clock delayed by 120 ps, so its setup slack degrades by 120 ps - the borrowed time is taken from the following stage, not created.
L4.explanation: This conservation is why useful skew is a local optimisation with a global budget. It works when a slow stage sits next to a fast one and fails when several consecutive stages are critical.

L4.prompt_tpl: Clock arrives at the launch flop at {tl} ps and at the capture flop at 400 ps. With clock-to-Q 150 ps, logic 2200 ps, setup 90 ps and a 2500 ps period, what is the setup slack? Answer with the setup slack in picoseconds.
L4.explanation: A capture clock that arrives after the launch clock effectively lengthens the period for that path. Note the same displacement subtracts directly from the hold slack, so the tool has to check both before accepting the skew.

concepts.t: Clock jitter and the timing budget
concepts.L1: Jitter is the cycle-to-cycle uncertainty in where a clock edge actually lands, caused by PLL noise, supply droop and crosstalk. In setup analysis it is subtracted from the available period as a pessimistic constant; unlike skew, it is statistical rather than deterministic.
concepts.L2: Jitter barely affects hold. A hold check compares launch and capture paths of the same edge, so a displacement of that edge hits both sides and largely cancels. Setup compares two consecutive edges, whose displacements are independent and add. A noisy supply therefore costs $f_{max}$ but rarely creates hold failures.
concepts.L3: Budgeting is why the two are kept separate. Skew is extracted from the clock tree and is per-path, so the tool applies the actual number for each launch-capture pair. Jitter is a global uncertainty applied as clock uncertainty, typically a few per cent of the period. With a 2500 ps period and 150 ps of jitter, the usable period is 2350 ps; a path needing $150 + 2200 + 90 + 120 = 2560$ ps then has $-210$ ps of slack, whereas without jitter it had $-60$ ps. In an SDC file you express this with `set_clock_uncertainty`, and if you forget it you will close timing in the tool and miss it on silicon - one of the most common causes of a chip that runs 10 per cent slower than the report promised.

L4.prompt_tpl: A 2500 ps clock has {j} ps of jitter. The path needs 2560 ps (clock-to-Q 150, logic 2200, setup 90, skew 120). What is the setup slack, and at what period would it just pass? Answer with the setup slack in picoseconds.
L4.answer: Slack = 2500 - j - 2560 = -60 - j. For j=0: -60 ps, needs T >= 2560 ps. For j=100: -160 ps, needs T >= 2660 ps. For j=150: -210 ps, needs T >= 2710 ps. For j=250: -310 ps, needs T >= 2810 ps.
L4.explanation: Jitter is a direct tax on the period. At 400 MHz a 150 ps jitter budget is 6 per cent of the cycle, which is why high-frequency designs spend real effort on PLL quality and supply decoupling rather than on more logic optimisation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does clock jitter degrade setup slack but have little effect on hold slack?
L4.answer: A setup check spans two consecutive clock edges, so the launch edge and the capture edge suffer independent displacements that add into the uncertainty. A hold check involves a single edge reaching both flops, so a displacement of that edge moves launch and capture together and cancels to first order. Only the uncorrelated part of the jitter between the two clock-tree branches matters for hold, and that is small.
L4.explanation: This is also why tools let you specify separate setup and hold clock uncertainty: set_clock_uncertainty -setup is usually several times larger than -hold, and using one number for both over-constrains hold and wastes buffers.

concepts.t: Metastability and the resolution time constant
concepts.L1: When a flop samples a changing input it can enter a metastable state - its output hovering between levels - and the time to resolve is unbounded, though exponentially unlikely to be long. The decay constant $\tau$ is a characterised property of the flop cell.
concepts.L2: The resolution time is genuinely unbounded, not merely large: no finite settling time gives certainty. The engineering question is never 'is this safe?' but 'what is the mean time between failures, against the product's life times the fleet size?' Ten million shipped units need an MTBF many orders of magnitude past one lifetime.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is the cross-coupled inverter pair inside the flop. Its stable states sit at the ends of a transfer curve whose middle has small-signal gain above one, so a disturbance grows as $v(t) = v_{0} e^{t/\tau}$ with $\tau$ the inverse of the loop gain-bandwidth product. Resolution happens when $v$ reaches a logic level, so the time needed is logarithmic in $1/v_{0}$, and $v_{0}$ is roughly uniform - which produces the exponential tail. Faster processes give smaller $\tau$. Most libraries ship dedicated synchroniser cells with $\tau$ minimised; using a plain flop instead can cost orders of magnitude of MTBF.

L4.prompt_tpl: With tau = 100 ps, by what factor does the probability of remaining unresolved fall if you allow {extra} ps more resolution time?
L4.answer: Factor = exp(extra / 100). For extra=200: e^2 = 7.389. For extra=500: e^5 = 148.41. For extra=1000: e^10 = 22026.47. For extra=2000: e^20 = 4.85e8.
L4.explanation: Resolution time buys reliability exponentially, which is why adding a single extra synchroniser flop typically multiplies MTBF by many orders of magnitude rather than merely doubling it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is there no circuit that eliminates metastability at an asynchronous boundary?
L4.answer: Because deciding which side of the setup/hold window an asynchronous edge fell on is a continuous-to-discrete decision with no guaranteed bounded resolution time. Any circuit that outputs a definite level in bounded time can be driven to its own metastable point by an adversarial input timing. This is a physical instance of the arbiter problem - proved unavoidable for bounded-time arbiters - so the only available engineering move is to make the failure rate arbitrarily small by allowing more resolution time.
L4.explanation: This is why the two-flop synchroniser is universal: it does not remove the hazard, it converts it into an MTBF number that can be made larger than the age of the universe for a cost of one flop.

prereqs: Setup time, hold time, and clock-to-Q

concepts.L1: MTBF for a synchroniser combines the exponential resolution term with how often the hazard is sampled: the product of the sampling clock frequency and the rate of asynchronous data transitions. It is the number that justifies calling a two-flop synchroniser safe.
concepts.L2: The frequencies enter linearly and the resolution time exponentially, which upends intuition. Halving the data toggle rate only doubles MTBF; adding one flop at 500 MHz multiplies it by $e^{20} \approx 4.85 \times 10^{8}$. The right response to a marginal synchroniser is another stage, never a slower interface.
concepts.L3: Work the numbers, because the scale is the lesson. At $f_{clk} = 500$ MHz, $f_{data} = 50$ MHz, $\tau = T_{0} = 100$ ps and $t_{su} = 100$ ps, the denominator is $100 \times 10^{-12} \times 5 \times 10^{8} \times 5 \times 10^{7} = 2.5 \times 10^{6}$ events per second. One flop gives $t_{r} = 2 - 0.1 = 1.9$ ns, so $\mathrm{MTBF} = e^{19}/2.5\times10^{6} = 71.4$ seconds - a chip that fails about once a minute. Two flops give $t_{r} = 3.9$ ns, $e^{39} = 8.66\times10^{16}$, MTBF $= 3.46\times10^{10}$ s, about 1098 years. Three flops give $5.3\times10^{11}$ years. That step from one minute to eleven centuries for the price of one flop is the entire argument for the two-flop synchroniser.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using MTBF = exp(t_r/tau) / (T0 * f_clk * f_data) with tau = T0 = 100 ps, f_clk = 500 MHz, f_data = 50 MHz and setup 100 ps, compute the MTBF in seconds for a {n}-flop synchroniser.
L4.answer: t_r = n*2000 - 100 ps; denominator = 2.5e6 per second. For n=1: t_r=1900 ps, exp(19)=1.78482e8, MTBF=71.39 s. For n=2: t_r=3900 ps, exp(39)=8.65934e16, MTBF=3.4637e10 s (1098 years). For n=3: t_r=5900 ps, exp(59)=4.20121e25, MTBF=1.6805e19 s.
L4.explanation: Each added stage multiplies MTBF by exp(T_clk/tau) = exp(20) = 4.85e8 here. That is why two stages is the universal minimum and three is used on very fast clocks or very high-reliability parts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A two-flop synchroniser at 500 MHz has an acceptable MTBF. The clock is raised to 1 GHz with the same flops. What is the most effective single change?
L4.answer: Add a third synchroniser flop
L4.explanation: Doubling the clock halves t_r per stage, cutting the exponent roughly in half, which costs many orders of magnitude of MTBF - far more than the linear factor of two from the higher f_clk in the denominator. A third stage restores the exponent. Reducing the data rate would only help linearly.
options: Halve the asynchronous data toggle rate
Add a third synchroniser flop
Increase the supply voltage

prereqs: Metastability and the resolution time constant

sections.note: the control half of every design; the datapath is the easy half

concepts.L1: A Moore machine's outputs depend only on the current state, so they change once per clock and are clean. A Mealy machine's outputs also depend on the present inputs, so it can react in the same cycle an input arrives, at the cost of a combinational input-to-output path.
concepts.L2: The real cost of Mealy is the interface contract, not glitching. A Mealy output is a path from an input pin to an output pin with no flop between, so two Mealy blocks facing each other can close a combinational loop through ready and valid - the reason AXI forbids `valid` from depending combinationally on `ready`.
concepts.L3: Count states to see the trade. Moore needs a dedicated state to emit an output that Mealy emits on the transition into it, so detecting 101 costs three Mealy states and four Moore states. Against that, every Moore output decodes a registered value, so its timing path starts at a flop and cannot glitch; a Mealy output inherits the arrival time of whatever input it reads, which may already be late in the cycle. The production compromise is a registered Mealy output: compute the Mealy function, flop it, and pay one cycle of latency for a clean interface.

L4.prompt_tpl: A sequence detector for the pattern {pat} with overlap allowed. How many states does a minimal Mealy implementation need, and a minimal Moore implementation?
L4.answer: Mealy needs one state per non-empty proper prefix of the pattern plus the start state, i.e. len(pat) states. Moore needs one more, len(pat)+1, for the state that emits the match. For '101': Mealy 3, Moore 4. For '1101': Mealy 4, Moore 5. For '11': Mealy 2, Moore 3.
L4.explanation: The extra Moore state exists purely to hold the output high, because a Moore output cannot be emitted on a transition. That one state is the whole structural difference between the two styles.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two blocks are connected with valid/ready. Block A drives `valid` combinationally from B's `ready`; block B drives `ready` combinationally from A's `valid`. What is wrong and what is the rule?
L4.answer: It is a combinational loop: valid depends on ready which depends on valid, so the netlist has a cycle with no flop in it and neither simulation nor STA can resolve it. The AXI rule is that a source must not wait for ready before asserting valid - valid must not depend combinationally on ready. A sink may make ready depend on valid, but then the source must not, and the standard fix is a skid buffer that registers one side.
L4.explanation: This is why the Mealy-vs-Moore distinction matters at interfaces rather than inside a block. Any protocol with bidirectional handshaking must forbid at least one of the two combinational dependencies, or two conforming blocks cannot be connected.

concepts.L1: State encoding decides how many flops hold the state and how expensive it is to decode. Binary minimises flops, one-hot minimises decode logic, and gray minimises simultaneous bit transitions - each optimises a different resource.
concepts.L2: On an FPGA one-hot is usually right, and the tool often converts to it whether you asked or not, because flops are abundant and LUT depth is scarce. On an ASIC that reverses for large machines: 64 one-hot flops are real area and leakage where 6 are not. Either way, the encoding you wrote is not necessarily the one you got.
concepts.L3: The decode argument is concrete. With one-hot, testing 'am I in state $k$' reads one flip-flop - zero logic levels. With binary it is a $\lceil \log_{2} N \rceil$-input AND, one or two levels. A 16-state machine is 16 flops with free decode against 4 flops with a 4-input compare per state. Next-state logic follows: a one-hot next-state bit is an OR of the transitions entering that state, shallow and wide. Gray is a different concern - not decode cost but sampling. One bit changes per step, so a sampler catching the value mid-transition reads the old or the new state, never a third that never existed.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a {n}-state FSM, how many flops does binary encoding need, how many does one-hot need, and how many logic levels does a single-state decode take in each? Answer with the number of binary-encoding flops.
L4.answer: Binary: ceil(log2 n) flops, decode is one comparator of that width, roughly 1-2 levels. One-hot: n flops, decode is 0 levels - just read the bit. For n=8: 3 vs 8 flops. For n=16: 4 vs 16. For n=64: 6 vs 64.
L4.explanation: The crossover is where flop area starts to dominate decode depth. On FPGAs, which have far more flops than a design usually needs, one-hot wins almost always; on an ASIC a 64-state machine is 64 flops of area and leakage for a saving of two logic levels.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which encoding is required for a counter whose value is sampled by logic in a different clock domain?
L4.answer: Gray
L4.explanation: Only gray guarantees that a single transition changes one bit, so a sampler that catches the value mid-change reads either the old or the new value. Binary can change all bits at once (7 to 8 is 0111 to 1000), and independently sampled bits can produce a value that never existed. One-hot changes two bits per step and has the same problem.
options: Binary
Gray
One-hot

concepts.L1: The three-block style separates the state register, the next-state function and the output decode into distinct always blocks. It makes the flop count obvious, keeps every combinational block latch-free, and lets a reviewer check each piece independently.
concepts.L2: The single-block style - next-state logic inside `always_ff` - is not wrong, but it registers every intermediate signal whether you meant it to or not, and it cannot express a Mealy output without extra plumbing. The three-block form's payoff is reviewability: any assignment to a `_q` signal outside block 1 is instantly a bug.
concepts.L3: Two conventions carry the safety. First, `state_d = state_q;` as the opening line means every path through the block assigns `state_d`, so no latch is inferred however many branches you forget, and the default behaviour - hold - is stated once. Second, the `_d` and `_q` suffixes make dataflow visible: `_d` is a combinational next value, `_q` is what a flop holds, and the only legal transfer between them is inside an `always_ff`. The lowRISC guide mandates both, plus `unique case` so simulation flags an unreachable encoding. The redundant `default` arm is what lets the machine recover from an illegal one.

L4.prompt_tpl: An FSM's next-state block reads `always_comb begin unique case (state_q) IDLE: if (start) state_d = RUN; RUN: state_d = DONE; endcase end`. Name every defect.
L4.answer: Three. First, state_d is not assigned when state_q is IDLE and start is 0, so a latch is inferred on state_d. Second, there is no default arm, so DONE and any illegal encoding also leave state_d unassigned, adding to the latch and preventing recovery. Third, unique case will report a simulation error when state_q is DONE because no arm matches. The fix is state_d = state_q as the first statement plus a default arm.
L4.explanation: The opening default assignment fixes the latch on its own, and the default case arm fixes recoverability. Both are cheap and both are mandated by the lowRISC style guide for exactly this reason.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does the three-block style put `state_d = state_q;` at the top of the combinational block rather than adding an else to every if?
L4.answer: Because it makes latch-freedom structural rather than case-by-case. With the default in place, every execution path through the block assigns state_d before it exits, so no reachable path can leave it unassigned no matter how many branches are added later. Enumerating else clauses gives the same result today but breaks the moment somebody adds a branch, which is exactly the maintenance failure the style is designed to prevent.
L4.explanation: The same idiom applies to every combinational block, not only FSMs: assign defaults to all outputs first, then override. It also documents the intended idle behaviour in one visible place.

concepts.L1: Any FSM whose state count is not a power of two has unreachable encodings. A safe FSM defines what happens if the register ever holds one - normally jumping to reset - so a single upset cannot leave the machine stuck outside its reachable graph forever.
concepts.L2: `unique case` and an `x` default pull opposite ways. `unique` tells simulation to complain when no arm matches, which you want; an `x` default tells synthesis the illegal codes are don't-cares, which creates the lockup. Use both and you get a design that reports the problem in simulation and cannot recover from it on silicon.
concepts.L3: Lockup is a graph property, not a probability. If the synthesised next-state function maps an illegal encoding to itself or into a cycle of illegal encodings, no input sequence returns the machine to a legal state - only reset does, and a stuck control FSM usually still holds a bus grant or a handshake, so nothing else progresses either. Five states in three bits leaves three illegal codes, and a don't-care default lets the minimiser give them any next state, self-loop included. `default: state_d = IDLE;` costs a few gates of decode and turns any single-bit upset into at most one wrong cycle. Safety-critical parts add a `$onehot` legality check and a protected state register.

L4.prompt_tpl: An FSM has {n} states encoded in the minimum number of binary bits. How many bits, and how many unreachable encodings? Answer with the number of unreachable encodings.
L4.answer: Bits = ceil(log2 n); unreachable = 2**bits - n. For n=5: 3 bits, 3 unreachable. For n=6: 3 bits, 2 unreachable. For n=9: 4 bits, 7 unreachable. For n=16: 4 bits, 0 unreachable.
L4.explanation: Only exact powers of two have no illegal encodings, and adding one state to a machine at a power-of-two boundary suddenly creates a large illegal set - going from 8 to 9 states creates seven codes that need a defined recovery.

L4.prompt_tpl: A control FSM in a fault-tolerant design uses `default: state_d = 'x;` and `unique case`. Describe the failure a single-event upset can cause, and give the two-part fix.
L4.answer: An SEU flips a state bit to an unreachable encoding. Synthesis has already treated those encodings as don't-cares, so the next-state function may map the illegal code to itself, leaving the FSM permanently outside its reachable graph while it still holds whatever handshake or bus grant it owned. Fix one: `default: state_d = IDLE;` so every encoding has a defined recovery path. Fix two: add a hardware legality check on the encoding - one-hot with `$onehot` or a parity-protected state register.
L4.explanation: This is a standard requirement in automotive and aerospace flows - ISO 26262 and DO-254 style processes ask specifically about behaviour under illegal state encodings, and 'the tool optimised it away' is not an acceptable answer.

sections.note: the syntax layer - drill it until it is automatic, then stop thinking about it

concepts.L1: `logic` is SystemVerilog's single four-state variable type; it replaces the Verilog-95 `reg`/`wire` split for almost every purpose. A `logic` may have exactly one driver. A `wire` is a net type whose only remaining job is resolving several drivers onto one signal.
concepts.L2: The name `reg` has misled two generations. It never meant register - it meant 'assigned inside a procedural block', and `reg y; always @(a) y = ~a;` is a plain inverter with no storage. Whether you get a flop depends entirely on the block being edge-sensitive, never on the declaration keyword.
concepts.L3: The relaxation `logic` makes over `reg` is that a variable may now take a single continuous assignment, so the declaration keyword no longer depends on how you plan to assign the signal. The single-driver restriction is the price, and it is a feature: a second driver on a `logic` is a compile error, catching the accidental double-drive that on a `wire` silently resolves to X. Real multiple drivers are now rare - internal tristate buses have all but vanished in favour of muxes - so `wire` survives mostly at pads and in legacy code. The lowRISC rule is exactly this: `logic` for synthesis, `wire` only when necessary.

L4.prompt_tpl: `reg [7:0] count; always @(posedge clk) count = count + 1;` A reviewer says this has two problems. What are they?
L4.answer: First, the assignment is blocking inside a clocked block, so any other block reading count in the same time step may see the new value or the old one depending on scheduling order - a race that can differ between simulators and between simulation and synthesis. Second, `always` is used where `always_ff` should be, so nothing checks that the block really is sequential and no tool verifies the assignment style. Write always_ff @(posedge clk) count <= count + 1;
L4.explanation: The `reg` keyword is a red herring: it neither causes nor prevents the register. The register comes from `@(posedge clk)`. That is exactly the point of the reg-does-not-mean-register rule.

L4.prompt_tpl: In new SystemVerilog RTL, when is `wire` genuinely required rather than `logic`?
L4.answer: When a signal has more than one driver that must be resolved, such as a tristate bus or an open-drain pad
L4.explanation: `logic` permits one continuous assign, so the old wire-for-assign rule is gone. Only multiple-driver resolution needs a net type. Since internal tristate buses have essentially disappeared from ASIC design, most modern RTL contains no `wire` at all outside the pad ring.
options: Whenever the signal is driven by a continuous assign
When a signal has more than one driver that must be resolved, such as a tristate bus or an open-drain pad
Whenever the signal crosses a module boundary

concepts.L1: SystemVerilog values are four-state: 0, 1, X for unknown or conflicting, and Z for undriven. X is a simulation construct, not a physical value - silicon holds a voltage that reads as 0 or 1. Reasoning about X is reasoning about what your simulator shows you, not about what the chip does.
concepts.L2: X-optimism is the dangerous direction. When a condition is X, RTL simulation quietly takes the else branch, so an uninitialised register can give a run that looks correct while the chip does something else. Gate-level simulation is X-pessimistic instead and spreads X widely, which is why RTL-clean designs light up at gate level.
concepts.L3: Two mechanisms produce the asymmetry. In RTL, `if (c)` with `c = 1'bx` is defined by the language to execute the else branch - a statement has no third outcome - so the unknown is silently resolved. At gate level the same condition drives a mux whose output comes from a four-state truth table, and X on the select gives X unless both data inputs agree, so the unknown spreads. Neither matches silicon, where the node sits at some voltage and the mux picks a definite side, possibly a different one on each power-up. The defence is not to reason about X at all: reset everything that matters, run with X-propagation checking enabled, and assert that key control signals are never unknown.

L4.prompt_tpl: `logic [3:0] a = 4'b01x{last}; logic [3:0] b = 4'b0100;` What are `a == b`, `a === b` and `a !== b`?
L4.answer: a == b is 1'bx, because bit 1 is x and 4-state equality propagates the unknown. a === b is 1'b0, because === compares bit patterns exactly and the bits differ. a !== b is 1'b1. This holds for last = z, 0 or 1 alike, since the x in bit 1 already forces == to x.
L4.explanation: The rule: use == in RTL where you want unknowns to propagate, and === only in testbenches and assertions where you are deliberately inspecting X and Z. === is not synthesisable, precisely because silicon has no X to compare against.

L4.prompt_tpl: An RTL simulation of a FIFO passes. Gate-level simulation of the same netlist fills with X and fails, and nothing in the netlist is wrong. What is the most likely explanation?
L4.answer: The FIFO's memory or a control register is not reset, so it starts as X. RTL simulation is X-optimistic: an if or case on an X condition takes a definite branch, so the unknown never spreads and the test passes. Gate level is X-pessimistic: the same X feeds real gate models whose 4-state tables emit X unless a controlling value blocks it, so it spreads. Both are artefacts - on silicon the flop holds a real voltage - but the gate-level run is the honest warning that behaviour depends on uninitialised state.
L4.explanation: This is one of the most common late-stage surprises in an ASIC project. The fix is to reset every control-path register and run RTL with X-propagation checking, not to add X-blocking logic that makes gate level quiet.

concepts.L1: A packed array is one contiguous vector that happens to have a shape, so it can be sliced, concatenated and assigned wholesale. An unpacked array is a collection of separate objects with no defined bit ordering between elements, so it cannot be treated as a vector.
concepts.L2: The variable indexed part-select is the syntax that matters day to day, because `v[i*8 : i*8+7]` is illegal - a range select needs constant bounds. `v[i*8 +: 8]` is the legal form and synthesises to a mux. Getting `+:` and `-:` backwards silently selects the wrong byte, a painful bug in packet-parsing RTL.
concepts.L3: Choose packed when you need the whole thing as a value: buses, register fields, anything crossing a port or entering an arithmetic expression. Choose unpacked when the elements are genuinely independent objects, above all memory arrays. `logic [31:0] mem [0:1023];` is the pattern synthesis recognises as a RAM, while the packed equivalent asks for 32768 addressable flops and will be built that way. The distinction is also a lint gate: assigning an unpacked array to a vector is an error rather than a silent reinterpretation, which is the safety a software engineer expects and Verilog-95 did not provide.

L4.prompt_tpl: `logic [31:0] v = 32'hDEADBEEF;` with `i = {i}`. What are `v[i*8 +: 8]` and `v[i*8+7 -: 8]`?
L4.answer: Both name bits [i*8+7 : i*8], so they are equal. For i=0 both are 8'hEF, i=1 both 8'hBE, i=2 both 8'hAD, i=3 both 8'hDE. +: counts upward from the base and -: counts downward from the base, so these two expressions describe the identical range.
L4.explanation: They are equivalent only because the bases were chosen to match. Writing v[i*8 -: 8] instead selects downward from i*8, i.e. bits [i*8 : i*8-7], which underflows at i=0 - a silent wrong answer rather than an error.

L4.prompt_tpl: `logic [1023:0][31:0] mem; always_ff @(posedge clk) if (we) mem[addr] <= wdata;` Synthesis reports 32768 flip-flops instead of inferring a RAM. Why?
L4.answer: mem is declared with two packed dimensions, so it is one 32768-bit vector, not an array of separately addressable words. Nothing about it matches a memory template, so every bit becomes a flop. The fix is to make the outer dimension unpacked: logic [31:0] mem [0:1023];
L4.explanation: An expensive one-character mistake. Memory inference works on specific declaration and access templates, and a fully packed declaration falls outside every vendor's template.

concepts.L1: A packed struct gives a bit vector named fields while keeping it assignable as a whole. It is the standard way to define bus transactions, instruction formats and configuration registers, because one declaration serves both the RTL and the wire layout.
concepts.L2: Member order fixes bit position, first member highest, and nothing warns you if you reorder members while another file still writes the raw vector. A packed struct should therefore be defined once in a package and used by every producer and consumer - it is only safer than a concatenation if it is the single source of truth.
concepts.L3: Packed structs are what make wide interfaces maintainable. Without them a 300-bit bus is a concatenation whose field boundaries live in a comment, and any width change silently shifts every downstream field. With them the compiler recomputes the layout, `$bits(instr_t)` gives the width, and a port declared with the struct type is checked. Packed unions add reinterpretation: `u.raw` and `u.fields` alias the same bits, which is how you serialise a struct onto a bus and destructure it at the far end without writing offsets by hand. The equal-width constraint is what makes that alias well defined - unlike a C union there is no padding and no implementation-defined layout.

L4.prompt_tpl: `typedef struct packed {{ logic [{a}:0] tag; logic [7:0] data; logic valid; }} pkt_t;` What is `$bits(pkt_t)`, and which bit positions hold `data`? Answer with the total width in bits.
L4.answer: Width is (a+1) + 8 + 1. data occupies bits [8:1], since valid is the last member and therefore bit 0, with data directly above it. For a=3: 13 bits, data at [8:1]. For a=7: 17 bits, data at [8:1]. For a=15: 25 bits, data at [8:1].
L4.explanation: Field positions count from the least significant member upward, so widening the first member grows the struct without moving later fields. Appending a member at the end shifts everything, which is why new fields are conventionally added at the top.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is a packed union restricted to members of identical width, when a C union is not?
L4.answer: Because a packed union is simultaneously a vector: every member maps onto the same fixed set of bits with no padding, so a narrower member would leave bits undefined when read through a wider one. A C union lives in memory with implementation-defined padding, and reading the wrong member there is undefined behaviour rather than a hardware question. In SystemVerilog the union is a wiring alias, and wiring has no padding.
L4.explanation: SystemVerilog also has unpacked and tagged unions which relax this, but neither is synthesisable. For RTL, packed and equal-width is the only useful form.

concepts.L1: An enum creates a named set of values with a chosen base type. In RTL it is the standard way to declare FSM states and opcode fields, because tools display the label in waveforms and coverage, and the type blocks accidental assignment from an unrelated vector.
concepts.L2: The type safety is one-directional and shallower than it looks. SystemVerilog blocks implicit assignment from a vector to an enum, but a cast pushes anything through unchecked, and no simulator flags one that produces an unlisted encoding. An enum documents intent and helps debug; it does not guarantee a legal state.
concepts.L3: Two defaults bite. First, an enum with no base type is `int`: 32 bits, two-state, so the state register cannot hold X, which destroys the very X-propagation checks that would have caught an unreset FSM. Always write `enum logic [N-1:0]`.
