Second, the auto-numbering rule is that an unlabelled member takes the previous value plus one, so inserting a member in the middle renumbers everything after it - harmless if all uses go through the enum, catastrophic if any encoding was baked into a testbench, a firmware header or a stored value. The methods exist for testbenches; `.name()` in particular turns an unreadable 3'b011 in a waveform into `S_WAIT`.

L4.prompt_tpl: `typedef enum {{IDLE, RUN, DONE}} state_e; state_e s;` inside an FSM. The design uses more flops than expected and X-propagation checks never fire on s. Why?
L4.answer: The enum has no base type, so it defaults to int: 32 bits and 2-state. The state register is 32 flops rather than 2, and because a 2-state type cannot hold X, an unreset or corrupted state can never appear as unknown in simulation. Fix: typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, RUN, DONE} state_e;
L4.explanation: Synthesis usually optimises the unused upper bits away, so the flop count may not be the visible symptom. The lost X-propagation is the real damage, and it is silent.

L4.prompt_tpl: `typedef enum logic [3:0] {{A = 4'h{v}, B, C, D}} tag_e;` What numeric values do B, C and D take? Answer with the numeric value of D.
L4.answer: Unlabelled members continue from the previous value plus one. For v=1: B=2, C=3, D=4. For v=5: B=6, C=7, D=8. For v=9: B=10, C=11, D=12.
L4.explanation: This continue-from-previous rule is why inserting a member in the middle of an enum renumbers every later member. Safe as long as every user goes through the enum name; a silent interface break the moment an encoding is written down anywhere else.

concepts.L1: Parameters are elaboration-time constants that let one module description produce many hardware instances. `localparam` is the same thing without the override, and it is what you use for any value derived from other parameters so a caller cannot make the derivation inconsistent.
concepts.L2: Declaring a derived width as `parameter` rather than `localparam` is a real defect, not a style nit: a caller can then write `#(.Depth(16), .AddrW(2))` and get a FIFO whose pointer is too narrow to address its own memory. It elaborates, it simulates plausibly on short tests, and it wraps early under load.
concepts.L3: Parameterisation is the only genuine code reuse in RTL - no templates, no run-time generics, no polymorphism. Everything resolves at elaboration, so a parameter can size an array, pick a generate branch and feed constant functions. It follows that each parameter set produces its own copy of the hardware: four FIFO widths give four independent blocks sharing nothing. Elaboration-time assertions are the matching safety net - a generate-if with `$error` is evaluated once parameters are fixed, so an illegal configuration fails the build instead of producing quietly wrong logic.

L4.prompt_tpl: A FIFO declares `parameter int Depth = {d}` and `parameter int AddrW = $clog2(Depth)`. A user instantiates it with `.Depth({d})` and `.AddrW(2)`. What breaks, and what is the one-word fix?
L4.answer: The pointer width becomes 2 bits regardless of Depth, so read and write pointers wrap after 4 entries while the memory holds Depth entries. Past 4 entries the FIFO overwrites live data, and the full/empty flags are computed from truncated pointers, so it silently corrupts under load. One-word fix: declare AddrW as localparam.
L4.explanation: Any value derivable from other parameters must be localparam. The rule is mechanical: if you can compute it, the caller must not be able to state it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does instantiating one parameterised module at three different widths produce three separate blocks of hardware rather than one shared block?
L4.answer: Because parameters resolve at elaboration, before any hardware exists. Elaboration produces one instance per distinct parameter set, each with its own array sizes, wire widths and generate branches. There is no run-time dispatch in hardware and nothing to share - the width of a wire is physical. Sharing would need a single instance wide enough for the worst case plus muxing and sequencing, which is a design decision you make explicitly.
L4.explanation: This is the concrete difference from software generics. A C++ template also instantiates per type, but there you pay only for the instantiations you call; in hardware you pay for all of them simultaneously, in area, all the time.

concepts.L1: `$clog2` is the constant function that turns a depth into an address width. Casting comes in three flavours - type, width and sign - each written with a tick before the parenthesis. Together they are how parameterised RTL keeps its widths consistent.
concepts.L2: The off-by-one is the trap: `$clog2(Depth)` bits index `Depth` entries but cannot represent the count `Depth` itself. A 16-deep FIFO whose occupancy counter is 4 bits wraps to zero when full and reports empty - the single most common FIFO bug. Occupancy needs `$clog2(Depth)+1` bits, or a separate full flag.
concepts.L3: The three casts do genuinely different things. A type cast converts the value, zero-extending an unsigned source. A width cast forces a fixed width, truncating the top bits with no warning unless lint is on - this is the one that silently loses data. A sign cast changes only how the same bits are read, so `8'hFF` becomes $-1$, not 255. In parameterised code the width cast is unavoidable, since a loop index assigned to a derived-width signal must be forced to that width. The discipline is to write it explicitly rather than let the context-determined width rule decide, and to promote lint width warnings to errors.

L4.prompt_tpl: A FIFO has depth {d}. How many bits for the pointer, how many for an occupancy counter covering 0 to {d} inclusive, and what is `$clog2` of {d}? Answer with the occupancy counter width in bits.
L4.answer: Pointer: `$clog2(d)` bits. Occupancy: `$clog2(d)+1` bits, equal to `$clog2(d+1)` when d is a power of two. For d=16: 4, pointer 4, occupancy 5. For d=8: 3 and 4. For d=1024: 10 and 11. For d=12: 4, pointer 4, occupancy 4 - the non-power-of-two case where the two formulas differ.
L4.explanation: Note d=12: `$clog2(d)+1` is 5, safe but a bit wasteful, while `$clog2(d+1)` is 4 and exact. For powers of two they coincide, which is why the discrepancy stays hidden until someone parameterises the depth to a non-power-of-two.

L4.prompt_tpl: With `logic [7:0] b = 8'h{h}`, what are `int'(b)` and `signed'(b)` as 32-bit ints?
L4.answer: int'(b) zero-extends an unsigned 8-bit value, so i is the plain numeric value. signed'(b) reinterprets the same 8 bits as two's complement before extension. For h=FF: i = 255, j = -1. For h=80: i = 128, j = -128. For h=7F: i = 127, j = 127.
L4.explanation: The rule: a type cast converts the value, a sign cast reinterprets the bit pattern. Confusing them is the source of most sign-extension bugs in fixed-point datapaths, and it stays invisible until the operand goes negative.

sections.note: the blocks that become hardware, and the scheduler that decides what you see

concepts.L1: `always_comb` declares a block as combinational and asks the tool to enforce it. It builds the sensitivity list automatically, runs once at time zero, and makes an inferred latch a compile error rather than a silent structure.
concepts.L2: The difference from `always @(*)` that actually bites is function calls. `always @(*) y = f(a);` is sensitive to `a` but not to whatever `f` reads internally, so changing a signal inside `f` does not re-evaluate the block and simulation diverges from synthesis. `always_comb` looks through the call.
concepts.L3: The single-writer rule is the other quiet benefit. SystemVerilog forbids any variable written by an `always_comb` from being written anywhere else, so the accidental double-drive that used to produce a silent X on a `wire` is now a compile error naming both writers. Combined with the time-zero execution - which means a combinational output is never left at X waiting for its first input event - and with mandatory latch reporting, `always_comb` converts three classes of latent simulation-versus-synthesis mismatch into build failures. There is essentially no reason to write `always @(*)` in new code, and the lowRISC style guide requires `always_comb`.

L4.prompt_tpl: `function automatic logic f(); return g_enable & data; endfunction  always @(*) y = f();` Simulation does not update y when g_enable changes, but the synthesised gates do. Why?
L4.answer: always @(*) builds its sensitivity list only from signals read syntactically in the block itself. The block reads nothing except the call to f, so the inferred list is empty or minimal and g_enable is not in it. Synthesis ignores sensitivity lists entirely and builds the combinational function, so the netlist is sensitive to g_enable and the simulation is not. always_comb infers the list through the function call and fixes it.
L4.explanation: This is a textbook simulation-synthesis mismatch: both are behaving as specified, and the specification is what is wrong. It is the strongest single argument for always_comb over always @(*).

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these is NOT a property that `always_comb` adds over `always @(*)`?
L4.answer: It prevents the block from being sensitive to signals it does not read
L4.explanation: always_comb adds inferred sensitivity through function calls, execution at time zero, mandatory latch reporting and a single-writer rule. Both forms are sensitive only to what the block reads - that is not a difference, and inferring too broad a list was never the failure mode.
options: It runs once at time zero
It prevents the block from being sensitive to signals it does not read
It makes an inferred latch a tool error

concepts.L1: `always_ff` declares a block as sequential logic. The tool checks that it is edge-triggered and that nothing else writes its variables, and the register comes from the edge in the event control, not from the keyword.
concepts.L2: Omitting `else` inside `always_ff` is correct and idiomatic - it infers a clock enable, because a flop holds by construction. The same omission in `always_comb` infers a latch and is a bug. Learning 'assign in every branch' as a universal rule produces needless else clauses that cost a mux in every clocked block.
concepts.L3: What `always_ff` cannot check is the thing that most needs checking: it does not require non-blocking assignment. `always_ff @(posedge clk) q = d;` compiles, and introduces exactly the race Cummings' non-blocking paper is about. The style guide, the linter and code review carry that rule, not the language. The event control encodes the other structural decision: `or negedge rst_n` makes the reset asynchronous, acting immediately rather than at the next edge, and omitting it makes it synchronous. Both are legitimate, but the choice must be uniform across a clock domain.

L4.prompt_tpl: `always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin if (!rst_n) q <= '0; else q = d; end` This elaborates. What is wrong?
L4.answer: The else branch uses a blocking assignment inside a clocked block. Any other process that reads q in the same time step may see the new value or the old one depending on the simulator's process ordering, so simulation results are not reproducible and can differ from the synthesised netlist, which always behaves as if the update were non-blocking. always_ff does not catch this - it only checks edge sensitivity and single-writer. Change = to <=.
L4.explanation: Verilator flags this as BLKSEQ and most commercial linters flag it too, but the language itself permits it. Non-blocking in every clocked block is a discipline enforced by tooling, not by the compiler.

L4.prompt_tpl: `always_ff @(posedge clk) if (en) q <= d;` has no else branch. What does this infer?
L4.answer: A flip-flop with a clock enable
L4.explanation: A flop holds its value when not written, so an omitted else in a clocked block means hold - which is exactly what an enable does. Adding `else q <= q;` describes the same hardware but often synthesises to a feedback mux rather than a native enable pin, costing area. The same omission in always_comb would infer a latch.
options: A transparent latch
A flip-flop with a clock enable
A flip-flop that clears when en is low

concepts.L1: `always_latch` declares that a block is intended to infer a level-sensitive latch. Its value is not what it builds - `always @(en, d)` builds the same thing - but that it makes intent explicit, so every other latch in the design is provably unintentional.
concepts.L2: The point of the keyword is the contrapositive. Once every deliberate latch is inside an `always_latch`, any latch reported anywhere else is by definition a bug, and the lint rule can be promoted to an error with no exceptions list. That is what turns 'no inferred latches' from a guideline into a gate.
concepts.L3: Latches are forbidden by tractability, not by physics. A latch is transparent while enabled, so a path arriving late in one cycle keeps propagating into the next - time borrowing. That is genuinely useful in custom datapaths, and some very high-frequency designs are built that way. The cost is that timing analysis can no longer treat stages independently: the tool must trace paths across latch boundaries and solve for consistent borrowing, which is slower to converge and far harder to debug. Standard-cell flows therefore ban latches from the data path and permit them only inside characterised clock-gating cells, which are instantiated rather than inferred.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given that `always_latch` and `always @(en, d) if (en) q <= d;` synthesise identically, what does the keyword actually buy?
L4.answer: It converts a design rule into a compiler-checked contract in both directions. always_latch errors if the block does not infer a latch, so a block marked as a latch really is one; and because every intentional latch is now marked, a latch reported in any always_comb or bare always block is unambiguously an accident. That lets the team promote the no-inferred-latch lint rule to a hard error with no waiver list, which is the actual goal.
L4.explanation: This intent-declaring pattern runs through SystemVerilog: always_comb, always_ff, always_latch, unique, priority. None of them changes the hardware; all of them let a tool check that the hardware matches what you claimed.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why do synchronous digital flows ban latches from data paths?
L4.answer: Latch transparency lets a path borrow time across the cycle boundary, so timing cannot be closed one stage at a time
L4.explanation: Latches are smaller than flops and perfectly functional, so area and correctness are not the objection. The problem is that transparency couples adjacent stages in the timing analysis, turning a local per-stage check into a global constrained solve that is slower to run and far harder to debug.
options: Latches consume more power than flip-flops
Latch transparency lets a path borrow time across the cycle boundary, so timing cannot be closed one stage at a time
Latches cannot be scan-tested at all

L0.body:
// THE rule: <= in every clocked block, = in every combinational block.
module shift (input logic clk, input logic d, output logic q1, q2);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    q1 <= d;      // non-blocking: RHS sampled now, LHS updated later
    q2 <= q1;     // reads the OLD q1 -> a 2-stage shift register
  end
endmodule

module wrong (input logic clk, input logic d, output logic p1, p2);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    p1 = d;       // blocking: p1 updated IMMEDIATELY
    p2 = p1;      // reads the NEW p1 -> ONE flop, not two
  end
endmodule

concepts.L1: A non-blocking assignment evaluates its right-hand side immediately but defers the update, so every statement in the block reads the values that existed at the clock edge. A blocking assignment updates at once, so later statements see the new value.
concepts.L2: The failure mode is not that blocking assignments are wrong, but that they are order-dependent. `q1 <= d; q2 <= q1;` and the reverse describe the same two flops; with `=` they describe different hardware. Synthesis follows statement order and simulation follows the scheduler, so once another block reads the signal they disagree.
concepts.L3: Non-blocking exists because hardware flops update simultaneously. At a clock edge every flop samples its input and drives its new output, and none sees another's new value - which is what `<=` models by splitting evaluation from update. Blocking models a wire, whose new value is visible immediately. Using the wrong one still simulates, and often simulates correctly in isolation, which is what makes it dangerous: the `wrong` module above simulates as one flop and synthesises as one flop, so a value-checking testbench passes while the design silently lost a pipeline stage. Cummings' SNUG paper 'Coding Styles That Kill!' is the canonical treatment.

L4.prompt_tpl: `always_ff @(posedge clk) begin a <= b; b <= a; end` with a={a}, b={b} before the edge. What are a and b after the edge, and what hardware is this?
L4.answer: The values swap: after the edge a holds the old b and b holds the old a. For a=1,b=0: a=0,b=1. For a=0,b=1: a=1,b=0. For a=1,b=1: unchanged. This is a legal two-flop swap and it is exactly what the hardware does, because both flops sample simultaneously. With blocking assignments the same two lines would give a=b and b=b, i.e. one flop and a lost value.
L4.explanation: The swap is the cleanest demonstration that non-blocking models simultaneity. There is no ordering of blocking assignments that produces a swap without a temporary, and hardware needs no temporary.

L4.prompt_tpl: A pipeline stage is written `always_ff @(posedge clk) begin stage1 = din; stage2 = stage1; dout = stage2; end`. The testbench passes but the latency is wrong on silicon. Explain.
L4.answer: Blocking assignments execute in order within the time step, so stage1 takes din, then stage2 immediately takes the new stage1, then dout takes the new stage2. The whole chain collapses to a single flop with one cycle of latency instead of three. Synthesis builds exactly that, so the netlist and the RTL agree - and the testbench, if it only checks data values rather than cycle-accurate timing, never notices. Replace every = with <=.
L4.explanation: This is the highest-value single rule in SystemVerilog RTL. It is also why lint rules for blocking assignments in clocked blocks are treated as errors, not warnings, in every serious flow.

concepts.L1: A simulation time step is not atomic: it is a sequence of ordered regions, and processes are scheduled into them. Non-blocking assignment works by splitting across two regions - evaluate in Active, update in NBA - which is precisely what removes read-write races between clocked blocks.
concepts.L2: This is why `$display` in a clocked block appears to lie. It executes in Active, before any NBA update has landed, so it shows pre-edge values for everything assigned with `<=`. `$strobe` is the fix: it defers to the Postponed region and prints the settled values, which is what a human reading a log expects.
concepts.L3: The regions are what make non-blocking assignment race-free rather than merely conventional. Take two clocked blocks, one doing `a <= b` and one `b <= a`. Both right-hand sides evaluate in Active using pre-edge values, and both updates apply in NBA, so the outcome does not depend on which process ran first. With blocking assignments both would complete inside Active and the result would depend on scheduler order, which the standard leaves undefined. The same mechanism explains why a clock generated with `<=` is safe against flops sampling it while one generated with `=` can race, and why testbench drivers conventionally drive stimulus with `<=` or on the opposite edge.

L4.prompt_tpl: Inside `always_ff @(posedge clk)`, a block does `count <= count + 1;` then a `$display` of count, then a `$strobe` of count. With count = {c} before the edge, what do the two print?
L4.answer: `$display` prints the old value c, because it runs in the Active region before the NBA update lands. `$strobe` prints c+1, because it runs in the Postponed region after all NBA updates for this time step have been applied. For c=5: 5 then 6. For c=0: 0 then 1. For c=41: 41 then 42.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common source of confusing simulation logs. The rule of thumb is $display for combinational tracing and $strobe for anything sampled on a clock edge.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two always_ff blocks in different modules do `a <= b;` and `b <= a;` on the same clock. Why is the result independent of which block the simulator runs first?
L4.answer: Because non-blocking assignment splits across regions. Both right-hand sides are evaluated in the Active region, where a and b still hold their pre-edge values, and both left-hand sides are updated in the NBA region afterwards. Whichever process runs first therefore reads the same values, so the swap is deterministic. With blocking assignments both statements would complete inside Active and the second to run would read the first one's new value, making the result depend on scheduler order that the standard leaves undefined.
L4.explanation: This determinism is the whole reason the NBA region exists. It is also why mixing blocking and non-blocking assignments to the same variable is undefined in practice even when a particular simulator produces a stable answer.

concepts.t: case, casez, and the unique/priority qualifiers
concepts.L1: `case` compares the selector against each arm in order. `casez` adds wildcard bits in the patterns so ranges can be matched. `unique` and `priority` are assertions about the arms that both simulation and synthesis consume.
concepts.L2: `unique` is a claim, not a construct, and a false claim is worse than none. If the arms are not actually exclusive, synthesis may drop the priority encoder and build a parallel mux, so the netlist takes a different branch from simulation - and the simulation error fires only if a test happens to hit the offending combination.
concepts.L3: `casex` is the one to ban outright. It treats an X in the selector as matching any arm, so during reset or before initialisation it can take a branch impossible on silicon, hiding the exact bug X-propagation was meant to expose. `casez` is safe because only the patterns carry wildcards, and it is the right tool for opcode decode where whole fields are irrelevant. `unique` versus `priority` maps onto hardware: `unique` licenses a flat one-hot mux, cheap and shallow, while `priority` requires a cascade whose depth grows with the arm count. `priority` on exclusive arms wastes area and delay; `unique` on overlapping arms is a correctness bug.

L4.prompt_tpl: `unique case (op) 4'b00??: y = A; 4'b0000: y = B; endcase` What is wrong, and what will simulation and synthesis each do?
L4.answer: The arms overlap: op = 4'b0000 matches both. The unique qualifier asserts they are mutually exclusive, so the claim is false. Simulation issues a unique-violation error when op is 0000 - but only if a test actually drives that value. Synthesis is entitled to trust the claim and build a parallel mux with no priority, so the netlist may select either A or B, and there is no requirement that it agree with the simulator's first-match rule. Also, a plain case does not treat ? as a wildcard - this needs casez.
L4.explanation: Two lessons: unique is an assertion you must be able to prove, and ? is a wildcard only under casez or casex. Both mistakes here are silent under the right test suite.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why should `casex` never appear in synthesisable RTL?
L4.answer: An X in the selector matches every arm, so an unreset signal can take a branch that is impossible on silicon
L4.explanation: casez wildcards only the patterns, which is safe and useful. casex additionally wildcards X and Z in the selector itself, so during reset or before initialisation the case takes an arbitrary branch and simulation quietly hides an X that silicon would have resolved to some definite, possibly different, value.
options: It is not supported by most synthesis tools
An X in the selector matches every arm, so an unreset signal can take a branch that is impossible on silicon
It always infers a latch

concepts.L1: A generate construct replicates hardware structurally at elaboration time. The loop index is a `genvar`, a compile-time constant, and each iteration produces its own instances, its own always blocks and its own hierarchy level.
concepts.L2: The block label is not cosmetic. It becomes part of the hierarchical path that timing constraints, formal properties and coverage exclusions reference. Unnamed blocks get `genblk1`, `genblk2` in source order, so inserting an unrelated conditional generate above them renumbers every downstream reference and breaks the SDC file.
concepts.L3: The distinction from a procedural `for` is what beginners get wrong. A `for` inside `always_comb` is also unrolled, but it produces logic within a single block and its index is a variable. A generate `for` produces separate named scopes, so it can contain module instantiations, `always_ff` blocks and declarations - things a procedural loop cannot. That is why an array of processing elements, a bank of memories or a parameterised prefix network must be a generate. Conditional generate is the other half: it selects which hardware exists at all, so a parameter can remove a debug port or a wide-mode datapath rather than leaving it to be optimised away.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why must a bank of N module instances be written as a generate for-loop rather than a for-loop inside always_comb?
L4.answer: Because a procedural for-loop is a statement, and module instantiation, always blocks and declarations are not statements - they are structural items that must appear at module scope. A generate loop unrolls into module scope and creates a named scope per iteration, so each iteration can hold an instance, its own always_ff and its own local signals. A procedural loop only replicates assignments inside the single block that contains it.
L4.explanation: The same rule explains why interface instances, assertions bound to each element, and per-element parameter overrides all require generate. If it creates hierarchy, it needs generate.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design has `for (genvar i = 0; i < {n}; i++) begin ... end` with no label, and an SDC file containing `set_false_path -from [get_pins genblk1[3]/*]`. A developer adds an unrelated `if (DEBUG) begin ... end` generate above it. Timing closure silently changes. Why?
L4.answer: Unnamed generate blocks are numbered genblk1, genblk2 and so on in source order. Adding a new unnamed conditional generate above the loop makes it genblk1, so the loop becomes genblk2 and the SDC path genblk1[3] now refers to something else or to nothing at all. The false path is silently no longer applied, or applied to the wrong logic, and no tool errors because get_pins on a non-matching pattern usually just returns an empty collection. Label every generate block.
L4.explanation: This is why the lowRISC style guide and Verilator's GENUNNAMED warning both insist on labels. It is also an argument for making empty SDC collections an error in your constraint scripts.

concepts.L1: A function computes a value with no notion of time and is synthesisable; a task may wait on events or delays and is therefore testbench-only. The `automatic` lifetime qualifier gives each invocation its own local storage.
concepts.L2: The default lifetime in a module is `static`, so two concurrent invocations of one task share a single set of locals. In a constrained-random testbench with several parallel drivers this produces corruption that looks like a design bug and reproduces only under particular timing. Declare everything `automatic`.
concepts.L3: Synthesisability follows directly from time control. A function body must complete within one evaluation of the enclosing expression, so it can only describe combinational logic, and synthesis inlines it. Any `@`, `#` or `wait` makes the construct a task and pushes it into the testbench. This is why a reference model written as a function can be shared between RTL and testbench - the same `gray_enc` above is used by the design and by the checker - while a bus driver must be a task. `function automatic void` is the useful middle case: no return value, no time control, so it can hold assertions and debug code and still be called from synthesisable contexts, where it is simply elaborated away.

L4.prompt_tpl: A testbench declares `task drive(input int id); repeat({n}) @(posedge clk); bus <= id; endtask` and forks {n} concurrent calls. The bus shows the wrong ids. Why?
L4.answer: The task is not declared automatic, so its lifetime is static and all concurrent invocations share one copy of the argument id. Each new call overwrites id for every call already in flight, so by the time an earlier call reaches its assignment it drives whichever id was written last. Declaring it `task automatic drive(...)` gives each invocation private storage and fixes it.
L4.explanation: Static lifetime is the Verilog-95 default that SystemVerilog kept for compatibility. It is a bug factory in any testbench with concurrency, and it is why style guides mandate automatic on every task and function.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which construct can appear inside a synthesisable function?
L4.answer: A for loop with compile-time-bounded iterations
L4.explanation: Functions must complete within one evaluation, so no event control, delay or wait is permitted - those make it a task. A statically bounded for loop is fine because synthesis unrolls it. A dynamically bounded loop cannot be unrolled and is rejected.
options: An @(posedge clk) event control
A for loop with compile-time-bounded iterations
A #10 delay

concepts.L1: An interface groups the signals of a protocol into one declaration that modules connect to as a single port. A modport names a role - source, sink, monitor - and fixes each signal's direction for that role, so the connection is type-checked.
concepts.L2: The synthesisable subset is narrower than the language. Interfaces holding only signals and modports are supported by every major synthesis tool; those holding tasks, clocking blocks or class handles are testbench-only. Mixing the two in one interface is a common way to get a design file that simulates and will not synthesise.
concepts.L3: The win is change cost. A five-signal AXI-Stream bus threaded through eight modules is forty port declarations, and adding a `tuser` field means editing all eight. With an interface it is one declaration and one edit. The modport makes this safe rather than merely convenient: without directions an interface is a bundle of nets, and two producers wired together silently multiply-drive. With `src` and `snk` modports the compiler knows `tvalid` is an output for one role and an input for the other, so a mis-wiring fails at elaboration. Clocking blocks extend the idea to testbenches with sampling and driving skews, but they are not synthesisable.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does adding modports to an interface prevent that a plain signal bundle does not?
L4.answer: It prevents direction errors at elaboration. Without modports every signal in the interface is bidirectional from each module's point of view, so connecting two producers to the same interface gives two drivers on tvalid and tdata, which resolves to X on a net or is a hard error only if the signals happen to be declared as variables. With modport src and modport snk, tvalid is an output for one role and an input for the other, so the second producer's assignment is a compile error naming the offending signal.
L4.explanation: This is the same single-writer discipline that `logic` and `always_comb` enforce, lifted to the protocol level. It is the main reason to prefer an interface over a struct plus a naming convention.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these makes an interface non-synthesisable?
L4.answer: A clocking block with input/output skews
L4.explanation: Signals and modports are the synthesisable subset that every major tool supports. Clocking blocks exist to define sampling and driving skews for testbench stimulus and have no hardware meaning. Parameters and generate constructs inside interfaces are fine.
options: A parameter on the interface
A clocking block with input/output skews
More than four signals in the bundle

sections.note: the handful of mistakes that produce hardware which simulates correctly and fails on silicon

concepts.L1: An inferred latch is storage the tool builds because your combinational description was incomplete. If some input pattern assigns nothing to an output, the only hardware that satisfies the description is one that remembers, so the synthesiser inserts a transparent latch.
concepts.L2: The usual advice - 'assign every output in every branch' - is the fragile fix. With eight outputs and six branches that is 48 assignments, and one omission reintroduces the bug. Assigning defaults once at the top of the block is provably complete no matter how the branches later change.
concepts.L3: The tool is not being clever or stupid; it is being literal. RTL semantics say a variable holds its value between assignments, so `case` with a missing arm specifies memory, and the smallest hardware with that behaviour is a latch. The reason this matters is timing, not area: a latch is transparent while enabled, so the static timing analyser can no longer treat each stage as bounded by two edges and must solve for time borrowing across the latch. Reports get slower, harder to read and sometimes non-convergent. The defence is layered - `always_comb` makes the infer an error, defaults at the top make it impossible, and lint promoted to a build gate makes it visible.

L4.prompt_tpl: This block synthesises a latch on `y`. Name the exact input value that creates it and give the one-line fix that survives later edits to the case arms.
L4.answer: sel == 2'd3 matches no case arm, so y is unassigned on that path and must hold - that is the latch. The edit-proof fix is a default assignment before the case, e.g. `y = 4'b0000;` as the first statement in the always_comb block, because it covers every present and future missing arm at once. Adding `default: y = 4'b0000;` inside the case also works today but has to be maintained alongside the arms.
L4.explanation: Verilator reports this exact form as %Warning-CASEINCOMPLETE; the same block written as `if (sel==0) y=...` with no else reports %Warning-LATCH instead. Both should be errors in your build, not warnings - a latch you did not ask for is never what you meant.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why do synthesis flows treat an inferred latch as a serious defect rather than a small area cost?
L4.answer: It makes static timing analysis solve for time borrowing instead of checking edge-to-edge paths
L4.explanation: The area of one latch is negligible. The cost is analytical: a transparent latch lets a late signal keep propagating into the next cycle, so timing paths no longer terminate at a flop and the tool must reason about borrowing across boundaries. That is slower, harder to debug, and the reason standard-cell flows ban latches outside characterised clock-gating cells.
options: A latch consumes more area than a flip-flop
It makes static timing analysis solve for time borrowing instead of checking edge-to-edge paths
Latches cannot be reset

prereqs: case, casez, and the unique/priority qualifiers

concepts.L1: An explicit sensitivity list is a simulation scheduling directive, not a hardware description. Synthesis ignores it entirely and builds the combinational function from the assignments, so a list missing a read signal makes the simulator lag behind the netlist.
concepts.L2: The failure is silent in the direction that hurts. Your testbench passes, because the simulator is the thing that is wrong, and the bug appears only in gate-level simulation or on the bench. This is the inverse of the usual debugging assumption that a passing test means working logic.
concepts.L3: Why no linter reliably catches it: `always @(a or b)` is a perfectly legal way to write sequential or event-driven logic, and IEEE 1364 has always permitted partial lists deliberately. A tool that flagged every partial list would flag every clocked block. Verilator's actual response is instructive - it reports BLKSEQ, a blocking assignment in what it classifies as a sequential process, because an explicit list is its only signal of intent. `always_comb` fixes this by construction: the list is inferred from the reads, including reads inside function calls, and latch and single-writer checks then apply.

L4.prompt_tpl: `always @(a or b) y = a & b & c;` with a=1, b=1, c=0 settled, then c rises to 1 with a and b unchanged. What is `y` in RTL simulation, and what is it in the synthesised netlist?
L4.answer: RTL simulation leaves y at 0: c is not in the sensitivity list, so the rise of c schedules no evaluation of the block and y keeps its stale value. The synthesised netlist gives y = 1, because synthesis discards the sensitivity list and builds a three-input AND gate whose output tracks c combinationally. The two disagree, and only gate-level simulation or silicon shows it.
L4.explanation: This divergence is the reason the mismatch is dangerous rather than merely wrong: the RTL testbench is green. Writing always_comb makes the list inferred and the two views agree by construction.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can a linter not simply warn 'signal c is read but not in the sensitivity list' the way a compiler warns about an unused variable?
L4.answer: Because an explicit sensitivity list is legal and meaningful for non-combinational processes. `always @(posedge clk)` and `always @(req or ack)` are event-driven descriptions in which reading a signal that is not an event trigger is exactly the intent. The tool has no way to know whether a partial list is an omission or the specification, so the warning would fire on every clocked block. Declaring `always_comb` supplies the missing intent, which is why the language added it.
L4.explanation: This is a general pattern in SystemVerilog: the 2005 additions - always_comb, always_ff, always_latch, unique, priority - add no hardware, they add declared intent so a tool can check the description against it.

concepts.t: Blocking assignment in a clocked block
concepts.L1: Blocking assignment executes like a software statement: evaluate, store, continue. Inside a clocked block that models a bank of flops, this makes downstream statements see values that only exist after the edge, describing hardware that does not exist.
concepts.L2: The order-dependence is worse than the collapse. Swap the three lines to `q2 = q1; q1 = q0; q0 = d;` and blocking assignment now builds the correct three-deep shift register. Code whose synthesised structure depends on statement order is code no reviewer can read.
concepts.L3: The deeper hazard is across blocks, not within one. Two `always_ff` blocks on the same edge, one writing `q` with `=` and one reading `q`, race: the language does not order independent processes, so the reader may see the pre-edge or post-edge value depending on the simulator's internal scheduling, and two simulators can legitimately disagree. Non-blocking assignment removes the race by construction - every non-blocking update is deferred to the NBA region, after every process in the time step has sampled its right-hand sides, so every reader sees the old value and the result is order-independent. `always_ff` does not enforce this; Verilator's BLKSEQ warning and the style guide do.

L4.prompt_tpl: `always_ff @(posedge clk) begin q0 = d; q1 = q0; q2 = q1; end` with d held at 1 and q0=q1=q2=0 before the edge. What are q0, q1, q2 immediately after one rising edge, and how many flops does this synthesise to?
L4.answer: q0=1, q1=1, q2=1 after a single edge, because each blocking assignment completes before the next statement reads it, so d propagates through all three in zero time. It synthesises to one flip-flop driving q2 (with q0 and q1 optimised away as wires), not the three-deep shift register the code appears to describe. With non-blocking assignment the result after one edge would be q0=1, q1=0, q2=0.
L4.explanation: The tell is that the answer changes if you reorder the three lines. Any construct whose hardware depends on statement order inside a clocked block is a bug, because a clock edge has no order.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two separate `always_ff @(posedge clk)` blocks, one containing `q = a;` and another containing `b <= q;`. Why is the value of b after the edge not determined by the language?
L4.answer: The two processes are independent and IEEE 1800 does not order their execution within a time step. If the writer runs first, its blocking assignment has already updated q, so the reader samples the new value; if the reader runs first, it samples the old one. Both orders are legal, so two simulators - or the same simulator on a different day - can produce different results, and neither is a bug in the tool. Making the write non-blocking removes the choice: the update is deferred to the NBA region after all sampling, so the reader always sees the old value, matching the netlist.
L4.explanation: This is exactly what Cummings' 'Nonblocking Assignments in Verilog Synthesis, Coding Styles That Kill!' is about. The rule <= in sequential, = in combinational is not stylistic; it is what makes simulation deterministic.

concepts.L1: Multiple drivers means two pieces of hardware are wired to the same net and both trying to set it. Verilog's `wire` type was designed for real tristate buses and quietly resolves the conflict; on-chip, outside a genuine tristate structure, it is a wiring fault.
concepts.L2: The bug rarely looks like this example. It usually appears as a signal assigned in two `always` blocks in two different files, or a port connected both by name and by an `assign` at the instantiation - and in four-state simulation it produces an X that propagates a hundred cycles before anything visibly breaks.
concepts.L3: The type system is the real fix, and it is why `logic` exists. A `logic` variable admits one continuous driver or one procedural writer, not both and not two of either, so the elaborator can name both offenders and stop. That converts a class of bug which used to surface as an unexplained X deep in a waveform into a build error with two file-and-line references. Genuine on-chip tristate is essentially extinct in modern standard-cell design - internal buses are muxes, and only pads are tristate - so almost every multiple-drive report is a mistake. Verilator reports it as MULTIDRIVEN and it should be an error in your build.

L4.prompt_tpl: A signal `busy` is declared `logic` and assigned by `always_comb` in one file and by a continuous `assign` in another. The design elaborates in a four-state simulator but the waveform shows `busy` stuck at X. Explain the X and say why declaring it `wire` would have hidden the problem rather than fixed it.
L4.answer: Two drivers are fighting: whenever one drives 0 and the other drives 1 the resolved value is X, so busy is X except when they happen to agree. Declaring it wire does not remove the second driver - it only makes the conflict legal, because wire resolution is defined for exactly this case, so the tool stops complaining while the netlist still contains two cell outputs shorted together. The fix is to delete one driver; keeping it as logic makes the elaborator name both.
L4.explanation: The general rule: use logic everywhere and reserve wire for the rare case where you genuinely want resolution, which on-chip is essentially only bidirectional pads.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is on-chip multiple driving a physical problem and not merely a modelling one?
L4.answer: Two cell outputs driving opposite values short the supply through both cells
L4.explanation: A standard-cell output is a CMOS push-pull stage. Two of them on one net with opposite values connect VDD to ground through two low-resistance paths - excess current, an indeterminate voltage, and possible damage. Four-state simulation's X is a polite abstraction of a real electrical fault, which is why tristate on-chip was replaced by muxes.
options: It doubles the net capacitance and slows the path
Two cell outputs driving opposite values short the supply through both cells
The synthesiser cannot compute the net's fanout

concepts.L1: Reset is a clock-domain crossing that people forget is one. Asynchronous assertion is what you want - the design must reset with no clock running - but asynchronous release is an unclocked event landing near a clock edge, with exactly the metastability risk of any other async input.
concepts.L2: Recovery and removal are setup and hold for the reset pin: recovery is how long before the clock edge the reset must be released, removal how long after it must stay asserted. Violating them leaves the flop metastable or, more often, lets parts of the design exit reset one cycle apart.
concepts.L3: The reset synchroniser above is the whole technique and it is deliberately asymmetric. The reset input goes to the asynchronous clear of both flops, so assertion is immediate and needs no clock. Release is not connected asynchronously at all - a constant 1 shifts through two flops, so `rst_n` rises two clock edges after `arst_n` does, aligned to the clock, and any metastability from the release lands on the first flop where it has a full cycle to settle. One synchroniser per clock domain, its output driving that domain's flops. On FPGAs the trade-off differs: flops initialise from the bitstream, so a broad reset net mostly costs routing and Fmax.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your chip has three clock domains at 500 MHz, 100 MHz and 32.768 kHz, all released by one external asynchronous reset pin. How many reset synchronisers do you need, and what breaks if you use one synchroniser in the 500 MHz domain and fan its output to all three?
L4.answer: Three - one per clock domain, each clocked by that domain's own clock. Sharing the 500 MHz synchroniser fails because its output changes on a 2 ns grid that is asynchronous to the 100 MHz and 32.768 kHz clocks, so from those domains' point of view the release is still an unclocked event arriving at an arbitrary phase, with the same recovery/removal risk you were trying to remove. The slow domain is the worst case: a release that misses its edge is not seen for another 30.5 us.
L4.explanation: The general statement: synchronising a signal into domain A does nothing for domain B. Each destination domain needs its own synchroniser, which is the same rule as for any other CDC signal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is the reset synchroniser built so that assertion is asynchronous but release is synchronous, rather than making both synchronous?
L4.answer: Assertion must work with no clock running; release has a clean edge to align to
L4.explanation: At power-up or after a clock failure there may be no clock, so a synchronous-only reset could never take effect - the design would come up in an arbitrary state and might never be clocked. Release is different: by then the clock is running, so the design can align the de-assertion to an edge and remove the recovery/removal hazard. The asymmetry follows from which events have a clock available.
options: Asynchronous release is faster than synchronous release
Assertion must work with no clock running; release has a clean edge to align to
Synchronous assertion would consume more area in the reset tree

concepts.t: X-optimism and initial values that die on ASIC
concepts.L1: X in simulation means 'unknown', but the simulator's rules for propagating it do not match silicon. An `if` on an X takes the else branch and produces a clean value, so unresolved state disappears from the waveform instead of spreading, and the bug it represents disappears with it.
concepts.L2: The same logic written two ways behaves differently. `if (x) y=a; else y=b;` yields a definite `b`, while `y = x ? a : b;` yields X. Neither models silicon, where the gate sees a real voltage and picks one branch deterministically per instance, per die, per temperature.
concepts.L3: This is why gate-level simulation still exists in an era of fast RTL simulators. After synthesis there are no `if` statements - only muxes, whose X behaviour is the pessimistic one - so state that RTL sim quietly resolved shows up as X spreading through the netlist, and a design that never resets its control flops usually fails within a few cycles. The discipline: reset every flop that can affect control flow or an external interface, leave datapath flops unreset if area demands it, and assert `$isunknown` on control signals so an X fails the test. FPGA users are most exposed - the bitstream really does initialise everything, so `initial` works perfectly until the RTL meets an ASIC.

L4.prompt_tpl: A control flop `mode` has no reset. In RTL simulation it is X at time 0. The design contains `if (mode) start_a(); else start_b();`. What does RTL simulation do, what does gate-level simulation do, and what does silicon do?
L4.answer: RTL simulation takes the else branch and calls start_b(), producing a clean deterministic-looking run that hides the bug. Gate-level simulation has a mux, not an if, so the X propagates into the outputs of start_a/start_b logic and the failure becomes visible. Silicon does neither: the flop powers up at a real voltage, so each instance picks a branch deterministically but unpredictably, and different dies or temperatures can pick differently - a chip that boots on the bench and hangs one unit in fifty in the field.
L4.explanation: The intermittent, unit-dependent failure is the signature. It is also why X-propagation modes and `$isunknown` assertions matter: they make RTL sim pessimistic on purpose so the bug surfaces before tapeout.

L4.prompt_tpl: The same RTL uses `initial cnt = 0;` and works on an Artix-7 FPGA. It is retargeted to a standard-cell ASIC and the counter comes up at a random value. What changed?
L4.answer: Nothing in the RTL - what changed is that on an FPGA the configuration bitstream writes every flop's initial value as part of loading the device, so the initial block is a synthesisable statement about the bitstream. A standard-cell ASIC flop has no such mechanism; it powers up in whatever state the transistors settle into, so ASIC synthesis ignores initial blocks entirely, usually with a warning nobody reads. The fix is a real reset: drive cnt from a reset synchroniser and clear it in the always_ff.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common surprise when FPGA-trained RTL meets an ASIC flow, and it is why the lowRISC style guide requires explicit reset of any state that matters rather than relying on initial values.

sections.note: the number one cause of chips that pass every simulation and fail intermittently at temperature

concepts.L1: A two-flop synchroniser is a shift register in the destination clock domain that buys one full clock period of settling time for a signal arriving with no defined phase relationship. Its output is a clean destination-domain signal, delayed by one to two destination cycles.
concepts.L2: It does not transport data - it transports one bit whose value is allowed to be sampled late. The first stage may resolve to either the old or the new value, so the synchroniser guarantees a legal value, not a particular one. Any protocol built on it must tolerate a one-cycle ambiguity.
concepts.L3: The fanout rule is the one people break. If `q[0]` drives three loads, each sees the metastable node through a different path with a different threshold, so during the resolution window two readers can latch opposite values - the design has lost the property that a wire carries one value. The first flop must drive only the second; fan out `q[STAGES-1]`, which is settled. The other half of the job is constraints: the input path crosses domains and is unanalysable, so it must be excluded with `set_false_path` or bounded with `set_max_delay -datapath_only`. Left unconstrained, the timing tool reports a meaningless violation - or meets it by accident and hides the crossing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A source domain runs at {fs} MHz and the destination at {fd} MHz. A pulse in the source domain must be at least 1.5 destination clock periods wide to be guaranteed sampled. How many source clock cycles wide must the pulse be?
L4.answer: cycles = ceil(1.5 * fs / fd). At 200 MHz source and 50 MHz destination: 1.5 * (1/50 MHz) = 30 ns, and one source cycle is 5 ns, so the pulse must be at least 6 source cycles wide. At 100/50 it is 3 cycles; at 200/25 it is 12.
L4.explanation: The 1.5 factor is the usual engineering margin: 1.0 periods can be missed if the pulse straddles an edge, so you need it comfortably wider than one destination period. This is precisely why single-cycle pulses cannot be synchronised directly into a slower domain and need a toggle synchroniser instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer synchronises `req` with two flops, then uses `q[0]` for a fast early-warning path and `q[1]` for the main logic, arguing that this saves a cycle of latency. What breaks?
L4.answer: q[0] is the metastable node. Tapping it puts a second load on it, so the two consumers see the unsettled voltage through different paths and can resolve to opposite values in the same cycle - the main logic sees req=0 while the early-warning path sees req=1, and the design's state machines diverge with no signal in the waveform to explain it. The synchroniser's guarantee applies only to its last stage; everything before it is explicitly not a logic value yet.
L4.explanation: This is the most common CDC review finding after 'no synchroniser at all'. If you need the signal a cycle earlier, add a stage and accept the latency, or restructure so the extra cycle does not matter.

concepts.t: Why a multi-bit bus cannot be bit-synchronised
concepts.L1: Independent synchronisers do not share a sampling instant. A bus whose bits change together is sampled by flops that each resolve independently, so the captured word is an arbitrary mixture of old and new bits - a value that may never have existed in the source domain.
concepts.L2: The failure rate is what deceives people. A binary counter crossing domains is wrong only during transitions, which is a small fraction of cycles, so a bit-synchronised bus can pass weeks of simulation and hours of bench testing and then corrupt one transaction an hour in the field at high temperature.
concepts.L3: Three structural answers exist and each fixes the problem differently. Gray coding removes it at the source: consecutive values differ in exactly one bit, so at most one synchroniser is in flight and the destination reads either the old value or the new one - both real. It works only for signals that move one step at a time, which is exactly what FIFO pointers do. A req/ack handshake removes it by making the data static: the source holds the bus until the synchronised `ack` returns, so no synchroniser ever samples a moving bit. An asynchronous FIFO combines both and is the general answer for continuous streams.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {w}-bit binary counter crosses clock domains through {w} independent two-flop synchronisers. On the single transition from all-ones to all-zeros, how many distinct values could the destination legally capture in that cycle?
L4.answer: 2**w. Every bit changes on that transition, and each synchroniser independently resolves to either the old bit or the new one, so any of the 2^w combinations of old and new bits is a legal capture. For w=3 that is 8, for w=4 it is 16, for w=8 it is 256. Exactly two of those (all-ones and all-zeros) are values the source actually held.
L4.explanation: This is the worst case, and it is the one a wrapping counter hits every 2^w counts. Gray coding reduces the count of simultaneously changing bits to one, so the number of legal captures drops from 2^w to 2 - and both are real values.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which crossing genuinely cannot be fixed by gray coding, and needs a handshake or a FIFO instead?
L4.answer: An arbitrary 32-bit data word that can change to any value at any time
L4.explanation: Gray coding only helps when consecutive values differ by one step, which is true of counters and FIFO pointers. Arbitrary data jumps anywhere, so no encoding makes successive values single-bit-adjacent; the data must instead be held stable while a single control bit crosses, which is what a handshake or an async FIFO does.
options: A FIFO write pointer that increments by one
An arbitrary 32-bit data word that can change to any value at any time
A binary counter that only ever counts up by one

concepts.L1: A toggle synchroniser converts an event into a level change, crosses the level, and converts it back to an event. Because a level persists until the next event, it cannot be missed by a slow destination clock the way a one-cycle pulse can.
concepts.L2: It silently drops events rather than reporting them. If two source pulses arrive closer together than roughly three destination periods, the level toggles twice before the destination samples, the two edges cancel, and both pulses are lost with nothing to indicate it happened.
concepts.L3: The toggle signal changes at most once per source event, so the crossing is single-bit and the synchroniser's guarantee applies directly. The edge detector recovers one destination pulse per toggle edge in either direction, which is why the XOR is of adjacent stages rather than a rising-edge detect. The throughput bound follows from synchroniser depth: two edges to see the level, one more to detect the change, so events must be spaced by about three destination periods. Fast-to-slow that is a real constraint, and the fix is a busy flag fed back through its own synchroniser - at which point you have built a handshake.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design uses this pulse synchroniser to cross an interrupt pulse from a 400 MHz domain to a 25 MHz domain. Under load the source issues two interrupt pulses two source cycles apart. What does the destination see, and why is nothing reported?
L4.answer: The destination sees nothing at all. Two source pulses toggle the level twice within 5 ns, while the destination clock period is 40 ns, so both toggles happen between two destination edges and the level returns to its original value before it is ever sampled. The edge detector finds no change, so both interrupts are silently lost. Nothing is reported because the mechanism has no acknowledgement path - the source never learns whether a toggle was observed.
L4.explanation: This is the throughput limit made concrete: events must be spaced by roughly three destination periods, here 120 ns or 48 source cycles. Guaranteeing that needs a busy flag returned through its own synchroniser, which turns the pulse synchroniser into a handshake.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is the recovered pulse produced by `s[2] ^ s[1]` rather than by a rising-edge detector such as `s[1] & ~s[2]`?
L4.answer: Because the source toggles the level on every input pulse, so consecutive events produce alternating rising and falling edges. A rising-edge detector would recover only every second pulse and drop the rest. The XOR of two adjacent synchroniser stages fires on any change, rising or falling, so each toggle yields exactly one destination-domain pulse regardless of the level's current polarity. The toggle encoding is what makes the crossing single-bit-safe; the XOR is what makes it polarity-agnostic.
L4.explanation: The same XOR-of-adjacent-stages idiom appears wherever a level crossing has to be turned back into an event, including in the gray-pointer comparisons inside an asynchronous FIFO.

concepts.t: The req/ack handshake and multi-cycle path formulation
concepts.L1: A handshake makes the data stationary rather than the crossing safe. Since the bus does not change while it is being sampled, no bit can be caught mid-transition and no synchroniser is needed on the data at all - only on the two single-bit control signals.
concepts.L2: The MCP formulation is a constraint, not a circuit. `set_max_delay -datapath_only` bounds the data path's raw delay while ignoring the clock relationship; a plain `set_false_path` would let synthesis route it arbitrarily long and break the stability assumption.
concepts.L3: Why the round trip has four phases rather than two: the source cannot lower `req` as soon as it sees `ack`, because the destination has not yet observed that `req` fell, and a new transfer starting immediately would be indistinguishable from the current one. The four-phase protocol returns both signals to zero before the next transaction, so each transfer is unambiguously delimited. Latency: `req` takes two destination cycles to synchronise, `ack` two source cycles to return, plus logic each side - roughly five destination cycles per word. Handshakes suit configuration registers, not streams.

L4.prompt_tpl: A four-phase handshake crosses a 32-bit configuration word. The source runs at 100 MHz, the destination at 40 MHz. Estimate the transfer latency in nanoseconds and the maximum sustainable transfer rate, and say why an async FIFO would beat it for streaming.
L4.answer: Roughly two destination cycles to synchronise req (2 * 25 ns = 50 ns), plus a destination cycle to capture and raise ack (25 ns), plus two source cycles to synchronise ack back (2 * 10 ns = 20 ns), plus a source cycle to drop req (10 ns), and the return-to-zero phase costs a similar amount again - call it 200 to 250 ns per word, so about 4 to 5 million words per second. An async FIFO wins because it does not serialise: the writer keeps writing while pointers cross, so throughput is set by the slower clock, roughly 40 million words per second here, an order of magnitude better.
L4.explanation: The rule of thumb is that a handshake costs about five destination cycles per transfer regardless of data width, so it is excellent for a 128-bit configuration word and terrible for a byte stream. Width is free; transactions are not.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is the data bus in a handshake constrained with `set_max_delay -datapath_only` rather than `set_false_path`?
L4.answer: False path lets the router make the data arbitrarily slow, breaking the stability assumption
L4.explanation: The handshake is correct only if the data has settled by the time the destination captures it, which is a real delay bound - about one destination period after req is synchronised. set_false_path removes the path from analysis entirely, so nothing stops synthesis routing it through a long detour and violating that bound silently. -datapath_only keeps the delay bound while ignoring the meaningless clock relationship.
options: False path is not supported on multi-bit buses
False path lets the router make the data arbitrarily slow, breaking the stability assumption
False path would remove the req and ack paths from analysis too

concepts.t: Gray pointers and the asynchronous FIFO
concepts.L1: An asynchronous FIFO lets two clock domains exchange a stream at full rate. Data lives in a dual-port memory that needs no synchronisation because writer and reader never touch the same address; only the pointers cross, gray-coded, one bit at a time.
concepts.L2: The pointer is one bit wider than the address. With $2^{AW}$ entries, empty and full both make the low $AW$ bits equal, so the extra most significant bit records how many times the pointer has wrapped and separates the two cases - full is 'gray pointers differ in the top two bits and match below', empty is plain equality.
concepts.L3: The safety argument turns on the direction of the error. Each side compares its own live pointer against a synchronised copy of the other side's, which is one to two cycles stale. A stale read pointer makes the FIFO look fuller than it is, so `wfull` asserts early; a stale write pointer makes it look emptier, so `rempty` asserts early. Both errors are conservative and neither can under-report, so overflow and underflow are impossible even though the comparison is always out of date. Gray coding is what makes the stale sample meaningful: one bit in flight means the synchronised value is either the previous pointer or the current one - both real states, not a fabricated mixture.

L4.prompt_tpl: A burst of {B} words is written at one word per cycle in a {fw} MHz domain, and drained at one word per cycle in a {fr} MHz domain. What is the minimum FIFO depth, and what depth would you actually build? Answer with the minimum FIFO depth.
L4.answer: depth = B - B*fr/fw, rounded up, then rounded to a power of two. For B=240, fw=200 MHz, fr=150 MHz: the burst takes 240/200 MHz = 1.2 us, during which 1.2 us * 150 MHz = 180 words drain, so 240 - 180 = 60 words must be buffered and you build a 64-deep FIFO (AW=6, 7-bit pointers). For B=512, fw=250, fr=100: 512 - 512*0.4 = 307.2, so 308 minimum and 512 built.
L4.explanation: Depth is set by the burst, not by the frequency ratio alone - a sustained rate mismatch cannot be fixed by any finite FIFO, so this calculation only makes sense when the average read rate is at least the average write rate.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer builds a 64-entry async FIFO with 6-bit gray pointers and defines `full = (wgry == rq2_wgry)` and `empty = (rgry == rq2_wgry)`. Both conditions are now identical. What did they get wrong and what is the fix?
L4.answer: They dropped the extra pointer bit. With 6-bit pointers for 64 entries, the pointers are equal both when the FIFO is empty and when it is exactly full after 64 writes, so the two conditions cannot be distinguished. The fix is 7-bit pointers: empty stays plain equality, while full is the write gray pointer equal to the synchronised read gray pointer with its top two bits inverted - the gray-code equivalent of 'same address, wrapped an odd number of times'. The top two bits rather than one because gray coding folds the two most significant binary bits together.
L4.explanation: This one-bit detail is the entire reason Cummings' asynchronous FIFO paper is long. Everything else in the design is a two-flop synchroniser and a memory; the pointer width and the full comparison are where it is actually possible to be wrong.
