sections.note: the boundary between a description that simulates and a description that becomes gates

concepts.L1: The synthesisable subset is the part of SystemVerilog that maps onto gates and flip-flops. The excluded constructs are excluded for one of three reasons: they reference wall-clock time, they need unbounded storage, or they are simulator services.
concepts.L2: Loops are the construct people misjudge. A `for` loop in synthesisable RTL is not a loop at all - it is unrolled at elaboration into that many copies of the hardware, so a loop bound of 1024 produces 1024 instances, not a sequencer. This is why the bound must be static and why an innocent-looking loop can explode the area.
concepts.L3: The dividing line is whether the construct has a meaning in a world with no clock but the one you declared. A `#10` delay says 'wait ten time units', which gates cannot do - only a counter clocked by something can, and you have to write that counter. A `while (fifo_not_empty)` says 'repeat an unknown number of times', which needs a state machine with a known number of states, and again you must write it. Classes need allocation. This is also why testbench code and design code are genuinely different languages inside one syntax, and why the lowRISC style guide separates them into different directories with different lint rules.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is `for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += a[i];` synthesisable when N is a parameter but not when N is an input port?
L4.answer: The loop is unrolled at elaboration, so the number of hardware copies must be known before the design exists
L4.explanation: Synthesis does not build a loop; it copies the body once per iteration and wires the copies together. That requires the trip count at elaboration time, which a parameter provides and an input port cannot - the port's value exists only at run time, when the gates already exist and their number is fixed. A data-dependent count needs an explicitly written state machine and an accumulator.
options: Input ports cannot be read inside a for loop
The loop is unrolled at elaboration, so the number of hardware copies must be known before the design exists
Parameters are constants so the tool can constant-fold the additions away

L4.prompt_tpl: A module contains `initial state = IDLE;` and no reset logic. It works perfectly on a Spartan-7 board through months of testing. It is ported to a standard-cell ASIC and the state machine sometimes enters an illegal state at power-up. What changed and what is the fix?
L4.answer: The FPGA bitstream writes every flop's initial value as it configures the device, so the initial block was effectively a reset. ASIC synthesis ignores initial blocks entirely - a standard-cell flop powers up in whatever state its transistors settle into, so the state register can come up in any encoding including unassigned ones. The fix is a real reset: bring in a reset synchroniser and clear state to IDLE in the always_ff, and add a default arm to the case so that an illegal encoding recovers rather than deadlocking.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common surprise when FPGA-trained RTL meets an ASIC flow, and it is why the style guides require explicit reset of any state that affects control flow, regardless of target.

prereqs: X-optimism and initial values that die on ASIC

concepts.L1: Inference describes what the hardware does and lets synthesis choose how to build it. Instantiation names a specific vendor cell. The first is portable and optimisable; the second is exact and frozen.
concepts.L2: An instantiated primitive is a black box to every downstream optimisation. The tool cannot retime through it, cannot resize it, cannot merge it with neighbouring logic, and cannot re-map it when you change device family - so an instantiation that gained ten per cent today can cost you the whole retiming pass tomorrow.
concepts.L3: The correct default is inference, and the correct exception list is short and structural. Clock generation cannot be inferred because there is no RTL expression for 'multiply this clock by 8 and phase-shift it' - an MMCM is a mixed-signal block, so it must be instantiated or generated by a wizard. I/O buffers are similar: the pad, its drive strength and its standard are physical properties with no behavioural description. Some hard-block features have no RTL form either, such as a DSP pre-adder or the cascade path between adjacent DSPs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these genuinely cannot be inferred from behavioural RTL and must be instantiated?
L4.answer: An MMCM that multiplies the input clock by 8 and phase-shifts it by 90 degrees
L4.explanation: Clock synthesis is a mixed-signal function - a phase-locked loop with analogue control - and there is no behavioural RTL that describes it, so it must be instantiated or generated. A block RAM and a DSP multiply-accumulate both have well-documented inference templates and should be written behaviourally so the tool can still retime and resize around them.
options: A 4096x32 simple dual-port block RAM
An MMCM that multiplies the input clock by 8 and phase-shifts it by 90 degrees
A pipelined 25x18 multiply-accumulate

L4.prompt_tpl: A team instantiates DSP48E1 primitives directly throughout an accelerator to guarantee the mapping. Two years later they port to a newer device family and to an ASIC. What does the decision cost them?
L4.answer: Every instantiation has to be rewritten. The newer family's DSP has a different name, different port list and different attribute set, so none of the instances elaborate, and an ASIC has no DSP48 at all - those instances must become inferred multipliers or library macros. Worse, during those two years the tool could not retime through any of the instances, could not merge adjacent arithmetic, and could not resize a multiplier when a datapath narrowed, so the design likely carries accumulated inefficiency as well. Inferred multiply-accumulates written to the vendor template would have mapped to the same DSP and survived both ports untouched.
L4.explanation: The general rule: instantiate what has no behaviour to describe, infer what does. The cost of instantiation is paid later and is invisible at the moment it looks like the pragmatic choice.

prereqs: Block RAM versus distributed RAM inference

concepts.t: Timing constraints and the SDC file

L0.body:
# constraints.sdc - the design's contract with the timing tool
create_clock -name clk_core -period 2.500 [get_ports clk]        ;# 400 MHz
create_clock -name clk_slow -period 20.000 [get_ports clk_s]     ;# 50 MHz

# Two unrelated clocks: tell the tool, or it analyses crossings
# as if they were phase-locked and reports meaningless failures.
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clk_core} -group {clk_slow}

set_clock_uncertainty 0.050 [get_clocks clk_core]   ;# jitter + margin

# Board-level timing: what the outside world guarantees and needs.
set_input_delay  -clock clk_core -max 0.900 [get_ports din*]
set_output_delay -clock clk_core -max 0.700 [get_ports dout*]

# An UNCONSTRAINED path is not analysed. It is not "fine" - it is
# invisible. Always check the report for unconstrained endpoints.

concepts.L1: An SDC file states the timing intent that RTL cannot express: how fast each clock runs, which clocks are related, how much uncertainty to allow, and what the world outside the chip guarantees at the pins. Static timing analysis checks the design against this file and nothing else.
concepts.L2: An unconstrained path does not pass - it is not examined. A missing `create_clock` means an entire clock domain goes unanalysed and reports zero violations, which is why the first thing to read in any timing report is the count of unconstrained endpoints, not the worst slack.
concepts.L3: The clock groups declaration is the one that has correctness consequences rather than just report quality. If two asynchronous clocks are left ungrouped, the tool assumes a common source and computes a worst-case phase relationship between them, then reports enormous violations on every crossing - and the usual response is to add a false path, which is right, or to accept the tool's suggestion of a large uncertainty, which hides the fact that the crossings needed synchronisers. Declaring the groups asynchronous states the truth and leaves the crossings to CDC analysis, which is the tool equipped to check them.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design has two clocks, and only one has a `create_clock`. The timing report shows zero violations. Why is this the most dangerous possible report?
L4.answer: Because the unconstrained domain was never analysed. Static timing analysis checks paths against clock definitions, so with no clock on the second domain, every path inside it and every path crossing into it has no required time and is simply skipped. Zero violations therefore means 'nothing was checked here', which is indistinguishable in the headline number from 'everything passed'. The design can be arbitrarily broken in that domain and the report will look perfect. The check is the unconstrained-endpoint count, which should be zero before any slack number is believed.
L4.explanation: This is the reason experienced engineers read a timing report from the coverage summary upward rather than from the worst path downward. A clean report on an incompletely constrained design is worse than a failing one, because it stops the investigation.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` between two clocks actually change in the analysis?
L4.answer: It stops the tool computing a phase relationship between them, so paths between the domains are not timed
L4.explanation: Without it, the tool assumes the clocks share a common ideal source and derives a worst-case alignment between their edges, producing large and meaningless violations on every crossing. Declaring them asynchronous says no fixed phase relationship exists, so cross-domain paths are excluded from setup and hold analysis and become the responsibility of CDC checking and the synchronisers you wrote. It does not add any hardware or make the crossings safe.
options: It inserts synchronisers automatically on paths between the domains
It stops the tool computing a phase relationship between them, so paths between the domains are not timed
It relaxes the required time on cross-domain paths by one full clock period

prereqs: The setup equation and maximum frequency
Clock jitter and the timing budget

L0.body:
Startpoint: u_ctrl/state_reg[2]  (rising edge-triggered, clk_core)
Endpoint:   u_dp/accum_reg[17]    (rising edge-triggered, clk_core)
Path Group: clk_core     Path Type: max (setup)

  Data arrival:
    clock clk_core rise                    0.000    0.000
    u_ctrl/state_reg[2]/C  (clock-to-Q)    0.121    0.121
    logic + net delay, 14 levels           2.043    2.164   <- arrival
  Data required:
    clock clk_core rise (period)           2.500    2.500
    clock network delay at endpoint       +0.080    2.580   <- skew
    clock uncertainty (jitter + margin)   -0.050    2.530
    library setup time                    -0.089    2.441   <- required
  ------------------------------------------------------------------
  slack (MET)                                       0.277

# slack = required - arrival = 2.441 - 2.164 = +0.277 ns
# Positive skew HELPED here: the capture edge arrives 80 ps late.
# The same 80 ps is subtracted in the HOLD check on this path.

concepts.L1: A timing report is an arithmetic statement. Arrival is when data actually gets to the capture flop; required is the latest it could get there and still be captured; slack is the difference, and a negative slack is a violation.
concepts.L2: The slack figure alone does not say what to fix. Fourteen levels of logic in 2.043 ns means the path is logic-bound and wants pipelining or restructuring; the same slack with three levels and 1.8 ns of net delay means it is routing-bound and wants floorplanning or replication - opposite remedies from one number.
concepts.L3: Skew appearing on both checks with opposite signs is the detail that unifies setup and hold. Here the capture clock arrives 80 ps after the launch clock, so the data has 80 ps longer to arrive - required time rises to 2.580 before the uncertainty and setup deductions bring it to 2.441, and slack is $2.441 - 2.164 = +0.277$ ns. The same 80 ps makes the hold check harder, because the data must still be stable 35 ps after a capture edge that is now late: with clock-to-Q 0.121 and a minimum logic delay of 0.052, arrival is 0.173 and the requirement is $0.080 + 0.035 = 0.115$, so hold slack is $+0.058$ ns.

L4.prompt_tpl: A path has clock period {T} ns, clock skew +{skew} ns at the capture flop, uncertainty 0.050 ns, clock-to-Q 0.121 ns, logic delay {logic} ns and library setup 0.089 ns. What is the setup slack? Answer with the setup slack in nanoseconds.
L4.answer: slack = (T + skew - 0.050 - 0.089) - (0.121 + logic). For T=2.500, skew=0.080, logic=2.043: required = 2.441, arrival = 2.164, slack = +0.277 ns. For T=2.000, skew=0.040, logic=1.900: required = 1.901, arrival = 2.021, slack = -0.120 ns, a violation. For T=4.000, skew=0.000, logic=3.500: required = 3.861, arrival = 3.621, slack = +0.240 ns.
L4.explanation: Note that the second case fails by 120 ps on a 2 ns period - a six per cent shortfall. That is the usual size of a real timing failure, which is why closure is a matter of restructuring one or two paths rather than redesigning the block.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two paths both report a setup slack of -0.100 ns. Path A has 18 levels of logic and 0.4 ns of net delay; path B has 3 levels and 1.9 ns of net delay. What distinguishes the correct fix?
L4.answer: A needs pipelining or logic restructuring; B needs floorplanning, replication or a shorter route
L4.explanation: The same slack arises from different causes. Path A's delay is in the gates, so cutting it needs a register inserted or the logic rebalanced - more levels than the period allows. Path B's delay is almost all interconnect, so adding pipeline stages barely helps; the cells are physically far apart, and the fixes are placement constraints, duplicating a high-fanout driver, or reducing the fanout that forced the long route.
options: Both need an extra pipeline stage, since slack is the same
A needs pipelining or logic restructuring; B needs floorplanning, replication or a shorter route
A is fixed by a slower clock; B is fixed by hold buffers

prereqs: The setup equation and maximum frequency
Timing constraints and the SDC file

L0.body:
# A FALSE path is never functionally exercised. Excluded entirely.
set_false_path -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b]
set_false_path -through [get_pins u_sync/q_reg[0]/D]      ;# 2FF sync input
set_false_path -from [get_ports test_mode]                ;# static config

# A MULTICYCLE path is real but is allowed more than one period.
# At 500 MHz (T = 2.000 ns), a 4-cycle multiply gets 8.000 ns:
set_multicycle_path 4 -setup -from [get_pins u_mul/a_reg*/C]                               -to   [get_pins u_mul/p_reg*/D]
set_multicycle_path 3 -hold  -from [get_pins u_mul/a_reg*/C]                               -to   [get_pins u_mul/p_reg*/D]

# The -hold 3 is NOT optional and is the classic error. Relaxing
# setup by N moves the HOLD check N-1 cycles later too, so without
# it the tool demands the data hold for 3 extra cycles and inserts
# an absurd amount of buffering - or reports a false failure.

concepts.L1: False and multicycle path exceptions tell the timing tool that the default single-cycle assumption is wrong for a particular path. They are the mechanism for expressing design intent that the netlist cannot show - and they are assertions you are responsible for.
concepts.L2: The `-hold` companion is not a refinement, it is required. `set_multicycle_path 4 -setup` alone shifts the hold check to three cycles after the launch edge, so the tool insists the launching data stay stable for three extra cycles - producing either a spurious violation or a design stuffed with delay buffers.
concepts.L3: The reason these exceptions are dangerous is that they are unverifiable by the tool. A false path declaration removes a path from analysis on your word that it is never exercised; if you are wrong, the path is unconstrained, the router is free to make it arbitrarily slow, and the chip fails in a way that no timing report ever showed. This is why the reset synchroniser and the CDC synchroniser inputs are the canonical legitimate false paths - their whole design assumption is that the path is unanalysable and metastability is handled structurally - while a false path added to make a report clean is a latent silicon bug.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design runs at {f} MHz. A multiply is allowed {n} cycles by a multicycle path exception. What setup window does the timing tool check against, and what hold multiplier must accompany it? Answer with the setup window in nanoseconds.
L4.answer: The setup window is n/f. At 500 MHz with n=4: T = 2.000 ns, window = 8.000 ns, and the exception must be accompanied by -hold 3, that is n-1. At 250 MHz with n=2: T = 4.000 ns, window = 8.000 ns, -hold 1. At 1000 MHz with n=8: T = 1.000 ns, window = 8.000 ns, -hold 7. The hold multiplier is always n-1 for a same-clock multicycle path.
L4.explanation: The n-1 arises because the exception moves the capture edge n cycles later for setup, and the hold check is defined relative to the capture edge one cycle before the setup capture - so it moves n-1 cycles too unless you say otherwise.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer clears a stubborn cross-domain violation with `set_false_path -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b]`. The report goes clean and the design fails intermittently on the bench at high temperature. What was the actual mistake?
L4.answer: The false path was the right constraint but it was applied instead of the fix rather than alongside it. Declaring the crossing unanalysable is correct - the clocks are asynchronous and no phase relationship exists - but it only silences the report; it does nothing about metastability. The paths crossing between the domains still need two-flop synchronisers on single-bit control signals and a gray-coded FIFO or handshake for anything multi-bit. The clean report was evidence that the tool had stopped looking, not that the crossing was safe.
L4.explanation: This is why set_clock_groups -asynchronous is preferred over blanket false paths for real CDC: it states the same fact but keeps the crossings visible to CDC analysis, which is the tool that can actually check for missing synchronisers.

L0.body:
# LEC proves netlist == RTL. It is not simulation and needs no vectors.
#   1. Map key points: every flop, port and black box in each design
#      must be matched by name or by structure.
#   2. For each matched output, prove the combinational cone feeding
#      it is Boolean-equivalent in both designs.
#   3. Report unmapped points and non-equivalent points.
#
# What it catches that simulation cannot:
#   a synthesis or DFT-insertion bug in a corner no test reached
#
# What breaks the mapping - and why each needs a setup directive:
#   retiming            flops MOVED, so key points do not correspond
#   FSM re-encoding     state bits mean something else
#   scan insertion      extra pins and a test-mode input
#   clock gating        an added enable term on the clock cone
#
# Unmapped key points are the real output. "0 non-equivalent" with
# 400 unmapped points proves almost nothing.

concepts.L1: Logic equivalence checking is a formal comparison of two versions of a design, typically RTL against the synthesised or post-layout netlist. It proves Boolean equivalence exhaustively, which no amount of simulation can, and it is a sign-off requirement in every ASIC flow.
concepts.L2: Its output is two numbers and only one gets read. 'Zero non-equivalent points' is meaningless without 'zero unmapped points' - an unmapped flop was not compared at all, so a run with hundreds of unmapped points has proved almost nothing while reporting success.
concepts.L3: The mapping step is where the real work is, and it is a direct consequence of what synthesis is allowed to do. Retiming physically relocates registers, so a flop in the netlist may correspond to no flop in the RTL and vice versa; the tool must be told to use sequential equivalence rather than point-to-point matching, which is a much harder problem. FSM re-encoding changes what the state bits mean, so a one-hot netlist register does not correspond to any binary RTL register. Scan insertion adds pins and a test-mode signal, and the standard setup is to constrain test mode inactive so the functional cones match.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can logic equivalence checking prove something that a hundred million simulation cycles cannot, and what can it not prove?
L4.answer: It compares Boolean functions symbolically rather than sampling them, so it establishes equivalence for all input combinations at once - including the ones no test vector ever produced. A hundred million cycles is a vanishing fraction of a design's input space, so simulation can only ever fail to find a difference. What LEC cannot prove is that the design is correct: it shows the netlist matches the RTL, so if the RTL has a bug, LEC confirms the bug was faithfully synthesised. It checks the transformation, not the specification.
L4.explanation: This division of labour is why both exist in a sign-off flow. Functional verification establishes that the RTL is right; equivalence checking establishes that nothing was lost between RTL and silicon.

L4.prompt_tpl: An LEC run reports 0 non-equivalent points and 400 unmapped points. What should the engineer conclude?
L4.answer: Almost nothing was proved, because unmapped points were never compared
L4.explanation: An unmapped key point is one the tool could not pair between the two designs, so its logic cone was excluded from the equivalence proof entirely. Four hundred of them means a large part of the design went unchecked - usually because retiming, FSM re-encoding or scan insertion moved or renamed state and the setup did not declare it. The correct next step is to fix the mapping, not to accept the zero.
options: The netlist is equivalent to the RTL and sign-off can proceed
Almost nothing was proved, because unmapped points were never compared
The 400 points are equivalent by default since none was reported non-equivalent

concepts.t: Lint, CDC checking, and the lowRISC style guide

L0.body:
$ verilator --lint-only -Wall --timing rtl/*.sv      # free, fast, strict
$ verible-verilog-lint --rules_config .rules.verible rtl/*.sv
$ verible-verilog-format --inplace rtl/*.sv           # settles style
$ sby -f fifo.sby                                     # formal, once you
                                                      # have properties

# The lowRISC / Google SystemVerilog style guide, used by OpenTitan
# and Ibex, is the de-facto open-source standard. The rules that are
# really bug prevention rather than taste:
#   always_comb / always_ff / always_latch  - never bare `always`
#   <= in sequential, = in combinational, never mixed in one block
#   `logic` everywhere; `wire` only for genuine multiple drivers
#   explicit reset for anything that affects control flow
#   _n suffix for active-low, _i/_o for direction, _q/_d for flop
#   no implicit width changes; no `.*` port connections
#
# STRUCTURAL CDC checkers (Questa CDC, Spyglass CDC, Conformal CDC)
# are a different tool class: they trace every crossing in the netlist
# and prove a synchroniser exists. Lint cannot do this - it is a
# whole-design structural analysis, and it has no free equivalent.

concepts.L1: Lint is the cheapest verification in the flow. Verilator's `--lint-only -Wall` finds inferred latches, blocking assignments in clocked blocks, multiple drivers, width mismatches and unused signals in seconds, on any size of design, for free.
concepts.L2: Style enforcement is not aesthetic. Most of the lowRISC guide's rules exist because the alternative permits a specific bug - `always_ff` rather than bare `always` makes edge sensitivity checkable, and the `_n` and `_q`/`_d` naming conventions make a polarity or stage error visible in review rather than in simulation.
concepts.L3: The tool categories are worth separating because their capabilities differ sharply. Lint is per-file and syntactic, so it catches everything in the classic-bugs list and nothing that requires understanding the whole design. Structural CDC analysis is whole-design and topological: it elaborates the netlist, identifies every path where a signal launched by one clock is captured by another, and checks that a recognised synchroniser structure sits on it. That analysis cannot be done file by file, which is why the commercial CDC tools are expensive and why there is no free equivalent - the closest open-source substitute is careful design convention plus formal properties on each crossing.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which defect can `verilator --lint-only -Wall` not find, no matter how the flags are set?
L4.answer: A single-bit control signal crossing clock domains with no synchroniser
L4.explanation: Lint analyses code structure within its view and reports latches, blocking assignments in clocked blocks, multiple drivers and width mismatches. Identifying a clock domain crossing requires elaborating the whole design, tracing which clock launches each signal and which captures it, and recognising synchroniser structures - a topological whole-design analysis that lint does not perform. That is the job of a structural CDC tool.
options: An inferred latch in a combinational block

L4.prompt_tpl: The lowRISC guide requires `_q` and `_d` suffixes on flop outputs and inputs. Name a concrete bug class this prevents and explain how.
L4.answer: It prevents accidentally reading the pre-flop combinational value where the registered one was intended, and vice versa - a one-cycle timing error that is invisible in the code and produces a subtle off-by-one in a protocol or a control sequence. With the convention, `count_d` is the value being computed this cycle and `count_q` is the value the flop holds, so a line reading `count_d` in logic that should have used `count_q` is visibly wrong to a reviewer without tracing the always_ff blocks. The naming makes the pipeline stage part of the identifier rather than something you have to reconstruct.
L4.explanation: This is the general argument for the naming rules in the guide: each one moves a class of error from something you find by simulating to something you find by reading. The _n suffix for active-low does the same for polarity inversions.

concepts.t: FPGA versus ASIC: what changes in the RTL
concepts.L1: FPGA and ASIC use the same language and diverge on economics. On an FPGA the fabric is fixed and free, so you design around the block sizes that exist; on an ASIC everything is buildable and everything costs area, power and mask money.
concepts.L2: The resets guidance points in opposite directions, which confuses people who learned one target first. FPGA advice is to minimise reset because the bitstream already initialises flops and a broad reset net eats routing; ASIC practice requires explicit reset because nothing else defines power-up state.
concepts.L3: Writing for the stricter target is the resolution, and it costs almost nothing. Explicit resets on control state work on both, and on an FPGA cost only a little routing on flops that would otherwise be initialised anyway. Avoiding `initial` for anything but block RAM contents works on both. No inferred latches and no gated clocks written in RTL work on both - and the ASIC's preferred clock gating is inserted by the tool from a clock-enable description, which is exactly what an FPGA wants too.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which single RTL habit causes the most porting failures from FPGA to ASIC?
L4.answer: Relying on initial values or bitstream power-up state instead of an explicit reset
L4.explanation: An FPGA writes every flop's initial value from the configuration bitstream, so RTL that depends on power-up state works perfectly and silently. ASIC synthesis discards initial blocks and standard-cell flops power up arbitrarily, so control state can start in any encoding, including illegal ones. The failure appears at power-up on silicon, which is the most expensive possible place to find it.

Writing multipliers behaviourally rather than instantiating DSP primitives

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is a 36-bit-wide FIFO often no more expensive than a 32-bit one on an FPGA, while on an ASIC it costs 12.5 per cent more memory area?
L4.answer: FPGA block RAM comes in fixed configurations - a RAMB36 offers 36-bit words because it carries a parity bit per byte - so a 32-bit design leaves four bits of each word unused and consumes exactly the same number of blocks as a 36-bit one. The resource is quantised, and you pay for the whole block either way. An ASIC memory is generated by a compiler to the requested dimensions, so every extra bit of width is extra bit cells, extra area and extra leakage in direct proportion. The FPGA rewards designing to the fabric's quantisation; the ASIC rewards using no more than you need.
L4.explanation: This is the clearest example of the general difference: FPGA resources are quantised and prepaid, ASIC resources are continuous and metered, and the same RTL is efficient on one and wasteful on the other.
